metadata.title: Generalized hyperbolicity for diffeomorphisms of Banach spaces

extraction_notes.note: Main theorem items (M1)-(M4) are proved in separate places and cited singly, so each is a claim nested in the theorem; proofs whose [Proof of Theorem (M_i)] argument names the whole theorem were pointed at the item claim.
Section 4 proof sketches: the sketch rule asks for rigor semi_formal, but rigor is forbidden on proof nodes; kept as proofs with alternative proves edges and no rigor field.
Section 4 contains a table of the four notions of generalized hyperbolicity (linear map, diffeomorphism, sequence, cocycle) and an omitted roadmap figure; neither was extracted as nodes.
Appendix B Propositions restate results of Robinson and Pilyugin, so they are external; the paper adds a justification which is recorded as paper proof nodes.

The justification of the uniform (C,lambda)-structure runs over three bold-headed paragraphs that also contain two quoted propositions; taken as one prose proof from 'The constants in this statement' to the end of the 'Return to the original metric' paragraph.

Discursive literature review in the introduction and the flows/semiflows part of Section 8 were not extracted; the introduction's result list is recorded only as also_stated_at where it repeats a result verbatim.
Unnamed prose inequalities derived in one sentence from the C^1 conditions were taken as claims containing their numbered equations.

nodes.name: Hyperbolic linear map
nodes.statement: An invertible linear map $T: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ is called hyperbolic if there exist $k > 0$ and a splitting $E^s \oplus E^u = \mathbb{R}^n$ such that \begin{equation} T E^s = E^s, \quad T E^u = E^u, \end{equation} \begin{equation} \mbox{$T|^k_{E^s}$, $T|^{-k}_{E^u}$ are contractions}. \end{equation}
differentia: there exist $k > 0$ and a splitting $E^s \oplus E^u = \mathbb{R}^n$ such that
nodes.statement_short: A linear map of R^n is hyperbolic if it has an invariant splitting on which T^k contracts on E^s and T^{-k} contracts on E^u.

nodes.name: Invariance of hyperbolic splitting (1)
nodes.statement: T E^s = E^s, \quad T E^u = E^u,
nodes.label: eq:HypIncl

nodes.name: Contraction on stable/unstable parts (2)
nodes.statement: \mbox{$T|^k_{E^s}$, $T|^{-k}_{E^u}$ are contractions}.
nodes.label: eq:HypContr

nodes.name: Grobman–Hartman theorem and properties of hyperbolic linear maps
nodes.statement: Such maps are known to be locally structurally stable (Grobman–Hartman theorem), to have the shadowing property, and to be expansive \cite{KatokHas}.
assumptions: Such maps
conclusions: are known to be locally structurally stable (Grobman–Hartman theorem), to have the shadowing property, and to be expansive

nodes.name: Banach space $\mathbb{B}$
nodes.statement: Throughout the paper, $\mathbb{B}$ denotes an arbitrary Banach space, with no reflexivity or separability assumption unless explicitly stated otherwise.
differentia: with no reflexivity or separability assumption unless explicitly stated

nodes.name: Generalized hyperbolic linear isomorphism
nodes.statement: We say that a linear isomorphism $T:\mathbb{B}\to\mathbb{B}$ is \textit{generalized hyperbolic} if there exists a splitting $\mathbb{B} = E^s \oplus E^u$ into two closed subspaces such that for some $k>0$ conditions~\eqref{eq:HypContr} hold and \begin{equation} T E^s \subset E^s, \quad T^{-1} E^u \subset E^u. \end{equation}
differentia: there exists a splitting $\mathbb{B} = E^s \oplus E^u$ into two closed subspaces such that for some $k>0$ conditions~\eqref{eq:HypContr} hold
nodes.statement_short: A linear isomorphism with a closed splitting whose stable part is forward-invariant, unstable part backward-invariant (inclusions only), with contraction.
nodes.label: def:genhyp

nodes.name: Generalized hyperbolic inclusions (3)
nodes.statement: T E^s \subset E^s, \quad T^{-1} E^u \subset E^u.
nodes.label: eq:GenHypIncl

nodes.name: Inclusions vs equalities in finite dimensions
nodes.statement: For finite-dimensional spaces $\mathbb{B}$, inclusions \eqref{eq:GenHypIncl} imply \eqref{eq:HypIncl}, but this is not so in the infinite-dimensional case.

nodes.name: Properties of generalized hyperbolic linear isomorphisms
nodes.statement: Generalized hyperbolic linear isomorphisms satisfy the shadowing property, and a Grobman-Hartman-type theorem. Their periodic orbits may be dense in the whole space and need not be expansive \cite{Puj18, Puj21, NilsonAli, Bernardes2026}.
assumptions: Generalized hyperbolic linear isomorphisms
conclusions: satisfy the shadowing property, and a Grobman-Hartman-type theorem
Their periodic orbits may be dense in the whole space and need not be expansive

nodes.name: Generalized hyperbolicity (diffeomorphism)
nodes.statement: We say that a diffeomorphism $f:\mathbb{B} \to \mathbb{B}$ satisfies \textit{generalized hyperbolicity} if there exist $C > 0$, $\lambda \in (0, 1)$ and a family of projections $P_x, Q_x: \mathbb{B} \to \mathbb{B}$ satisfying the following. Denote $E^s_x = P_x(\mathbb{B})$, $E^u_x = Q_x(\mathbb{B})$. \begin{itemize} \item[(GH1)] \textbf{Splitting.} For all $x \in \mathbb{B}$, $P_x + Q_x = Id$, $\|P_x\|, \|Q_x\| \leq C$. In particular $E^s_x \oplus E^u_x = \mathbb{B}$. \item[(GH2)] \textbf{Inclusion.} The subspaces $E^s_x$ and $E^u_x$ are invariant under the forward and backward iterations of $Df$, respectively: $$ Df(x)E^s_x \subseteq E^s_{f(x)}, \; D(f^{-1})(x)E^u_x \subseteq E^u_{f^{-1}(x)}, \quad \mbox{ for any $x \in \mathbb{B}$}. $$ \item[(GH3)] \textbf{Exponential estimates.} For any $x \in \mathbb{B}$, $n > 0$ $$ |Df^n(x)v^s_x| \leq C \lambda^n |v^s_x|, \quad v^s_x \in E^s_x; $$ $$ |D(f^{-n})(x)v^u_x| \leq C \lambda^n |v^u_x|, \quad v^u_x \in E^u_x. $$ \end{itemize}
differentia: \textbf{Inclusion.} The subspaces $E^s_x$ and $E^u_x$ are invariant under the forward and backward iterations of $Df$, respectively:
nodes.statement_short: A diffeomorphism of B is generalized hyperbolic if there are bounded projections P_x,Q_x with Df-forward-invariant stable and backward-invariant unstable subspaces (inclusions) and uniform exponential estimates; no continuity of x -> P_x.
nodes.label: def:CLf

nodes.name: Finite-dimensional characterization
nodes.statement: For a $C^1$-diffeomorphism of a smooth compact manifold, the tangent-bundle analogue of generalized hyperbolicity is equivalent to Axiom~A and the strong transversality condition.
also_stated_at: For a $C^1$-diffeomorphism of a smooth compact manifold, generalized hyperbolicity is equivalent to Axiom~A together with the strong transversality condition (Theorem~\ref{stat:finite-dimensional-characterization}).
assumptions: For a $C^1$-diffeomorphism of a smooth compact manifold
conclusions: the tangent-bundle analogue of generalized hyperbolicity is equivalent to Axiom~A and the strong transversality condition
equivalent_conditions: the tangent-bundle analogue of generalized hyperbolicity
Axiom~A and the strong transversality condition
nodes.statement_short: On a compact manifold, generalized hyperbolicity of a C^1 diffeomorphism is equivalent to Axiom A plus strong transversality.
nodes.label: stat:finite-dimensional-characterization

nodes.name: Uniform global $C^1$ conditions
nodes.statement: More precisely, assume that there exist $R>0$ and a nondecreasing function $r:\mathbb{R}^+\to\mathbb{R}^+$ such that \begin{equation} |f(x+v) - f(x) - Df(x)v| \leq |v|r(|v|), \quad x, v \in \mathbb{B}, \end{equation} \begin{equation} \|Df(x)\| \leq R, \quad \|D(f^{-1})(x)\| \leq R, \quad x \in \mathbb{B}, \end{equation} \begin{equation} \|Df(x+v) - Df(x)\| \leq r(|v|), \quad x, v \in \mathbb{B}, v \ne 0, \end{equation} \begin{equation} \quad \lim_{z \to 0} r(z) = 0. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Uniform global C^1 assumptions: remainder bound by |v|r(|v|), Df and D(f^{-1}) bounded by R, Df uniformly continuous with modulus r -> 0.

nodes.name: Class $\mathfrak{D}(\mathbb{B})$
nodes.statement: We denote by $\mathfrak{D}(\mathbb{B})$ the set of $C^1$-diffeomorphisms $f:\mathbb{B}\to\mathbb{B}$ satisfying \eqref{eq:C1-1}--\eqref{eq:C1-r2}.

nodes.name: Extended uniform $C^1$ distance
nodes.statement: We equip this set with the extended uniform $C^1$ distance $$ \|f-g\|_{C^1} := \sup_{x\in\mathbb{B}}|f(x)-g(x)| + \sup_{x\in\mathbb{B}}\|Df(x)-Dg(x)\|, \qquad f,g\in\mathfrak{D}(\mathbb{B}). $$
nodes.statement_short: Sup distance of maps plus sup operator-norm distance of derivatives, possibly infinite.

nodes.name: Elementary properties
nodes.statement: Let $f, h \in \mathfrak{D}(\mathbb{B})$ and assume that $f$ satisfies generalized hyperbolicity with constants $C>0$, $\lambda \in (0,1)$ and splitting $\mathbb{B} = E^s_x \oplus E^u_x$. Then: \begin{itemize} \item[(P1)] $\mathfrak{D}(\mathbb{B})$ is a group under composition, and $g = h \circ f \circ h^{-1}$ satisfies generalized hyperbolicity with constants $R_h^2 C$ and $\lambda$, where $R_h$ bounds $\|Dh\|$ and $\|Dh^{-1}\|$; \item[(P2)] $f^{-1}$ satisfies generalized hyperbolicity with the same constants and with the splitting obtained by interchanging $E^s_x$ and $E^u_x$; \item[(P3)] for every $n \geq 1$, $f^n$ satisfies generalized hyperbolicity with constants $C$, $\lambda^n$ and the same splitting; \item[(P4)] let $p \in [1,+\infty]$ and let $f_i \in \mathfrak{D}(\mathbb{B}_i)$, $i \in \mathcal I$, satisfy $f_i(0) = 0$, conditions \eqref{eq:C1-1}--\eqref{eq:C1-r2} with $R$ and $r$ independent of $i$, and generalized hyperbolicity with $C, \lambda$ independent of $i$. Then $f(\{x_i\}) = \{f_i(x_i)\}$ belongs to $\mathfrak{D}(\mathbb{B})$, where $\mathbb{B} = \bigl(\bigoplus_{i \in \mathcal I} \mathbb{B}_i\bigr)_{\ell^p}$, and satisfies generalized hyperbolicity with constants $C, \lambda$. \end{itemize}

nodes.name: Semiflows of parabolic and delay equations lie outside the category
nodes.statement: The semiflows of parabolic and delay equations that partly motivate this work belong to a different analytical category: they are typically non-invertible and generated by unbounded, densely defined operators, so \eqref{eq:C1-2}--\eqref{eq:C1-r1} do not apply as stated. Extending generalized hyperbolicity to that setting requires additional ideas and is left for future work; we return to this question in Section~\ref{sec:discussion}.

nodes.statement: For an interval \begin{equation} I=(a, b) \subset \mathbb{Z} \quad \mbox{with $a \in \mathbb{Z} \cup\{-\infty\}, b \in \mathbb{Z} \cup\{+\infty\}$} \end{equation} denote $\tilde{I} = \{k \in \mathbb{Z}: k, k+1 \in I\}$.

nodes.name: $d$-pseudotrajectory
nodes.statement: For $d>0$, we say that a sequence $\left\{y_{k} \in \mathbb{B}\right\}_{k \in I}$ is a $d$-pseudotrajectory if \begin{equation} \operatorname{dist}\left(y_{k+1}, f\left(y_{k}\right)\right) \leq d, \quad k \in \tilde{I}. \end{equation} If the interval $I$ is not specified, we assume that $I = \mathbb{Z}$.

nodes.statement: \operatorname{dist}\left(y_{k+1}, f\left(y_{k}\right)\right) \leq d, \quad k \in \tilde{I}.

nodes.name: Backward pseudotrajectory estimate
nodes.statement: By \eqref{eq:C1-2}, for any $d$-pseudotrajectory $\{y_k\}_{k \in I}$, the following inequality holds \begin{equation} |y_{k} - f^{-1}(y_{k+1})| \leq Rd, \quad k \in \tilde{I}. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Chain-recurrent point
nodes.statement: We say that a point $x \in \mathbb{B}$ is chain-recurrent for a diffeomorphism $f$ if, for any $d>0$, there exists a finite $d$-pseudotrajectory $\{y_k\}_{k \in [0, N]}$ with $y_0 = y_N = x$. Denote the set of all chain-recurrent points by $CR(f)$. Note that $CR(f)$ is closed.
nodes.section: 2.3 Shadowing, density of periodic points, and robustness

nodes.name: Set of periodic points $Per(f)$
nodes.statement: For $f \in \mathfrak{D}(\mathbb{B})$, denote by $Per(f)$ the set of periodic points.

nodes.name: Finite Lipschitz shadowing property (FinLipSh)
nodes.statement: We say that $f$ has the \textit{finite Lipschitz shadowing property} (FinLipSh) if there exist $M, d_{0} > 0$ such that for any $d < d_{0}$, finite interval $I = (a, b)$, and $d$-pseudotrajectory~$\left\{y_{k}\right\}_{k \in I}$ there exists an exact trajectory~$\{x_{k}\}_{k \in I}$ satisfying $|x_{k} - y_{k}| \leq M d$, $k \in I$.
nodes.section: 2.3 Shadowing, density of periodic points, and robustness

nodes.name: Lipschitz shadowing property (LipSh)
nodes.statement: We say that $f$ has the \textit{Lipschitz shadowing property} (LipSh) if there exist $M, d_{0} > 0$ such that for any $d < d_{0}$ and $d$-pseudotrajectory $\left\{y_{k}\right\}_{k \in \mathbb{Z}}$ there exists an exact trajectory $\left\{x_{k}\right\}_{k \in \mathbb{Z}}$ satisfying $|x_{k} - y_{k}| \leq M d$, $k \in \mathbb{Z}$.
nodes.section: 2.3 Shadowing, density of periodic points, and robustness

nodes.name: Lipschitz periodic shadowing property (LipPerSh)
nodes.statement: We say that $f$ has the \textit{Lipschitz periodic shadowing property} (LipPerSh) if there exist $M, d_{0} > 0$ such that for any $d < d_{0}$ and periodic $d$-pseudotrajectory $\left\{y_{k}\right\}_{k \in \mathbb{Z}}$ with $y_{k+N} = y_k$ (for some $N > 0$) there exists a periodic exact trajectory $\left\{x_{k}\right\}_{k \in \mathbb{Z}}$ satisfying \begin{equation}\notag x_{k+N} = x_k, \quad |x_{k} - y_{k}| \leq M d, \quad k \in \mathbb{Z}. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 2.3 Shadowing, density of periodic points, and robustness

nodes.name: Finite Lipschitz shadowing equals Lipschitz shadowing in finite dimensions
nodes.statement: For finite-dimensional spaces, the finite Lipschitz shadowing property is equivalent to the Lipschitz shadowing property.
nodes.section: 2.3 Shadowing, density of periodic points, and robustness
assumptions: For finite-dimensional spaces
conclusions: the finite Lipschitz shadowing property is equivalent to the Lipschitz shadowing property

nodes.name: Main theorem
nodes.statement: Let $f\in\mathfrak{D}(\mathbb{B})$ satisfy generalized hyperbolicity. Then: \begin{enumerate}[ label=\textup{(M\arabic*)}, ref=\textup{M\arabic*} ] \item $f$ has the Lipschitz shadowing property; \item $f$ has the Lipschitz periodic shadowing property; \item periodic points are dense in the chain-recurrent set: $\overline{Per(f)}=CR(f)$; \item generalized hyperbolicity is robust in the uniform $C^1$ distance: if $f$ satisfies generalized hyperbolicity with constants $C>0$ and $\lambda\in(0,1)$, then, for every $\lambda_1\in(\lambda,1)$, there exist $\delta>0$ and $C_1>0$ such that every $g\in\mathfrak{D}(\mathbb{B})$ satisfying $ \|g-f\|_{C^1}<\delta $ is generalized hyperbolic with constants $C_1$ and $\lambda_1$. \end{enumerate}

conclusions: $f$ has the Lipschitz shadowing property

nodes.name: Structural stability (uniform)
nodes.statement: We say that $f \in \mathfrak{D}(\mathbb{B})$ is \textit{structurally stable} if for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists $d_0 = d_0(\varepsilon) > 0$ such that for any diffeomorphism $g \in \mathfrak{D}(\mathbb{B})$ with $\|f-g\|_{C^1} < d_0$ there exists a continuous map $h_1: \mathbb{B} \to \mathbb{B}$ satisfying $\sup_{x \in \mathbb{B}}|h_1(x)| < \varepsilon$ such that $(Id+h_1)$ is a homeomorphism and $g \circ (Id+h_1) = (Id+ h_1) \circ f$. If, moreover, the map $h_1$ can be chosen so that $Id+h_1$ and $(Id+h_1)^{-1}$ are uniformly continuous, we say that $f$ is \textit{uniformly structurally stable}.
nodes.statement_short: f is structurally stable if every C^1-close g is conjugate to f by a near-identity homeomorphism Id+h_1; uniformly if Id+h_1 and its inverse are uniformly continuous.

nodes.name: Generalized hyperbolicity implies structural stability
nodes.statement: Every diffeomorphism $f \in \mathfrak{D}(\mathbb{B})$ satisfying generalized hyperbolicity is structurally stable.
assumptions: Every diffeomorphism $f \in \mathfrak{D}(\mathbb{B})$ satisfying generalized hyperbolicity
conclusions: is structurally stable
nodes.label: conj:SS-general

nodes.name: Uniformly continuous generalized hyperbolicity
nodes.statement: We say that $f \in \mathfrak{D}(\mathbb{B})$ satisfies \textit{uniformly continuous generalized hyperbolicity} if it satisfies generalized hyperbolicity with a family of projections $\{P_x, Q_x\}$ for which the maps $x \to P_x$, $x \to Q_x$ are in addition uniformly continuous, i.e. \begin{equation} \mbox{$\forall$ $\varepsilon > 0$ $\exists$ $\delta > 0$ such that $\|P_x - P_y\|, \|Q_x - Q_y\| < \varepsilon$ for $|x-y| < \delta$}. \end{equation}
differentia: the maps $x \to P_x$, $x \to Q_x$ are in addition uniformly continuous

nodes.name: Uniform continuity of projections (12)
nodes.statement: \mbox{$\forall$ $\varepsilon > 0$ $\exists$ $\delta > 0$ such that $\|P_x - P_y\|, \|Q_x - Q_y\| < \varepsilon$ for $|x-y| < \delta$}.
nodes.label: eq:cont-PQ

nodes.name: Uniform semi-structural stability
nodes.statement: We say that $f \in \mathfrak{D}(\mathbb{B})$ is \textit{uniformly semi-structurally stable} if for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there exists $d_0 = d_0(\varepsilon) > 0$ such that for any diffeomorphism $g \in \mathfrak{D}(\mathbb{B})$ with $\|f-g\|_{C^1} < d_0$ there exist uniformly continuous maps $h_1, h_2: \mathbb{B} \to \mathbb{B}$ satisfying $ \sup_{x \in \mathbb{B}}|h_1(x)|, \; \sup_{x \in \mathbb{B}}|h_2(x)| < \varepsilon, $ such that $$ g \circ (Id + h_1) = (Id + h_1) \circ f, \quad f \circ (Id + h_2) = (Id + h_2) \circ g. $$
nodes.statement_short: Every C^1-close g is semi-conjugate to f both ways by uniformly continuous near-identity maps Id+h_1, Id+h_2.
nodes.label: def:semi-SS

nodes.name: Semi-structural and structural stability
nodes.statement: If $f \in \mathfrak{D}(\mathbb{B})$ satisfies uniformly continuous generalized hyperbolicity, then there exist $M>0$, $d_0 > 0$ such that for any $d \in (0, d_0)$ and diffeomorphism $g \in \mathfrak{D}(\mathbb{B})$ with $\|f-g\|_{C^1} < d$ the following holds. \begin{enumerate}[ label=\textup{(S\arabic*)}, ref=\textup{S\arabic*} ] \item There exist uniformly continuous maps $h_1, h_2:\mathbb{B} \to \mathbb{B}$ satisfying \begin{equation} g \circ (Id+h_1) = (Id + h_1) \circ f, \end{equation} \begin{equation} f \circ (Id+h_2) = (Id + h_2) \circ g, \end{equation} \begin{equation} |h_1(x)|, |h_2(x)| < Md, \quad x \in \mathbb{B}, \end{equation} hence $f$ is uniformly semi-structurally stable. \item If additionally the spaces $E^s_x \oplus (Df(x))^{-1}E^u_{f(x)}$ do not depend on $x$, then $h_1$, $h_2$ can be chosen such that \begin{equation} (Id+h_1) \circ (Id+h_2) = Id, \quad (Id+h_2) \circ (Id+h_1) = Id. \end{equation} In that case, the maps $(Id+h_1)$, $(Id+h_2)$ are homeomorphisms, and hence $f$ is uniformly structurally stable. \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Compatibility condition is automatic for invariant splittings
nodes.statement: The additional condition in Theorem~\ref{thm:SS}\,(\ref{item:SS-full}) is automatic for an invariant hyperbolic splitting. Indeed, if $ Df(x)E_x^u=E_{f(x)}^u, $ then $ (Df(x))^{-1}E_{f(x)}^u=E_x^u, $ and consequently $ E_x^s\oplus(Df(x))^{-1}E_{f(x)}^u = E_x^s\oplus E_x^u = \mathbb{B}. $

nodes.name: Comparison with Lani-Wayda's results
nodes.statement: In \cite{LaniWayda1995} strong results on shadowing and stability (persistence in their terminology) were obtained. At the same time, their proof strongly relies on an expansivity argument, which is not available in our setting. For other cases in which uniqueness or expansivity simplifies the analysis of the interplay between shadowing, structural stability, and hyperbolicity or exponential dichotomy, see, for example, \cite{Henry94}.
nodes.label: rem:LaniWaydaResults

nodes.name: Nonlinear shift on $\ell^p(\mathbb{Z})$
nodes.statement: Let $\lambda \in (0, 1)$, $R > 1/\lambda$, $M > 1$ and diffeomorphisms $a_k: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ satisfy \begin{equation} a_k(0) = 0; \quad a'_k(x) \in \left(\frac{1}{\lambda}, R\right), \; k < 0; \quad a'_k(x) \in \left(\frac{1}{R}, \lambda\right), \; k \geq 0, \end{equation} \begin{equation} a_k \in C^2, \quad |a''_k|, |(a^{-1}_k)''| \leq M. \end{equation} Let $\mathbb{B} = \ell^p(\mathbb{Z})$ with $p \in [1, +\infty]$ and consider the map $f: \mathbb{B} \to \mathbb{B}$ defined as $$ f(\{x_k\}) = \{y_k\}, \quad \mbox{where $y_{k+1} = a_k(x_k)$}. $$ Then $f$ is a diffeomorphism satisfying generalized hyperbolicity.

nodes.name: Nonlinear shift is generalized hyperbolic

nodes.name: Proof that the nonlinear shift is generalized hyperbolic
nodes.statement: By the definition of $f$, the inequalities $|y_{k+1}| \leq R |x_k|$ hold, hence $\|f(\{x_k\})\| \leq R \|\{x_k\}\|$, and $f$ is well-defined. Moreover, $f^{-1}$ is defined by $f^{-1}(\{y_k\}) = \{x_k\}$, where $x_k = a_k^{-1}(y_{k+1})$, with $\|f^{-1}(\{y_k\})\| \leq R\|\{y_k\}\|$; hence $\{x_k\}$ is well-defined. For $\{x_k\} \in \mathbb{B}$ define a linear operator $A(\{x_k\}):\mathbb{B} \to \mathbb{B}$ by $$ A(\{x_k\})\{v_k\} = \{w_k\}, \qquad \mbox{where $w_{k+1} = a'_k(x_k)v_k$}. $$ It is invertible, with $A^{-1}(\{x_k\})\{w_k\} = \{v_k\}$, where $v_k = w_{k+1}/a'_k(x_k)$, and by \eqref{eq:shift-ak} we have $\|A(\{x_k\})\|, \|A^{-1}(\{x_k\})\| \leq R$. Let us show that $Df(\{x_k\}) = A(\{x_k\})$, where $Df$ is a Fréchet derivative. Indeed, \begin{multline*} f(\{x_k\} + \{v_k\}) - f(\{x_k\}) - A(\{x_k\})\{v_k\} = \{z_k\}, \\ \mbox{where $z_{k+1} = a_k(x_k + v_k) - a_k(x_k) - a'_k(x_k)v_k$}. \end{multline*} According to \eqref{eq:shift-akc2}, we have $|z_k| \leq M|v_k|^2$ and hence inequality \eqref{eq:C1-1} holds with $r(|v|) = M|v|$. Similarly, equation \eqref{eq:C1-r1} holds and $r$ satisfies \eqref{eq:C1-r2}. Let us show that $f$ satisfies generalized hyperbolicity. Denote $$ E^s = \{ v_k = 0, k < 0 \}, \quad E^u = \{ v_k = 0, k \geq 0 \}. $$ Note that $E^s \oplus E^u = \mathbb{B}$. Let $P_x, Q_x$ be the projections onto $E^s$ and $E^u$ respectively (independent of $x$). Then $ E^s_x = P_x(\mathbb{B}) = E^s$, $E^u_x = Q_x(\mathbb{B}) = E^u$, and $\|P_x\| = \|Q_x\| = 1 $, so condition (GH1) holds with $C \geq 1$. By construction, $A(x)E^s \subset E^s$ and $A^{-1}(x)E^u \subset E^u$, hence condition (GH2) holds. By \eqref{eq:shift-ak} we have $\|A(x)|_{E^s}\|, \|A^{-1}(x)|_{E^u}\| \leq \lambda$, and hence condition (GH3) holds with $C = 1$ and the same $\lambda$ as above.
nodes.section: 3.1 Strict invariant inclusions: a nonlinear shift
nodes.statement_short: Compute Df as the linear weighted shift A, verify the C^1 bounds, then check (GH1)-(GH3) for the constant coordinate splitting.

nodes.name: Consequences of the shift construction
nodes.statement: For every $p\in[1,+\infty]$, all conclusions of Theorem~\ref{thm:main-results} hold. Since the splitting is constant, it satisfies the additional hypothesis of Theorem~\ref{thm:SS}\,(\ref{item:SS-full}); hence $f$ is uniformly structurally stable.
nodes.section: 3.1 Strict invariant inclusions: a nonlinear shift

nodes.name: Strict inclusions and nonexpansivity of the shift
nodes.statement: Both inclusions in (GH2) are strict. For instance $A^{-1}(x)E^u \subsetneq E^u$, the missing direction being $e_{-1}$. Indeed, $A(x)e_{-1} = a_{-1}'(x_{-1})\,e_0 \in E^s$, so the unstable direction $e_{-1}$ is carried by $Df$ into the stable indices and $|A^n(x)e_{-1}| \to 0$ instead of growing. Similarly, $A(x)E^s \subsetneq E^s$, the missing direction being $e_0$. In particular, $f$ is not expansive, and the shadowing trajectory in Theorem~\ref{thm:main-results}\,(\ref{item:main-LipSh}) need not be unique. Thus strict invariant inclusions, nonexpansivity, and nonunique shadowing are compatible with uniform structural stability.
nodes.section: 3.1 Strict invariant inclusions: a nonlinear shift
nodes.statement_short: Both GH2 inclusions are strict for the shift (missing directions e_{-1}, e_0), so f is not expansive and shadowing is nonunique.

nodes.name: Nonuniqueness of the splitting
nodes.statement: The generalized-hyperbolic splitting is itself not uniquely determined by the dynamics. For every $N\in\mathbb{Z}$, one may take $C=R^{|N|}$ and \[ E_x^s=\{v_k=0,\ k<N\}, \qquad E_x^u=\{v_k=0,\ k\geq N\}, \] with the corresponding coordinate projections.
nodes.section: 3.1 Strict invariant inclusions: a nonlinear shift

nodes.name: Rates $\lambda_1<\lambda_2$
nodes.statement: Fix $0<\lambda_1<\lambda_2<1$.
nodes.section: 3.2 Discontinuous splittings and varying index: products of Morse-Smale maps

nodes.name: Morse–Smale map $a$ of the line
nodes.statement: Consider an increasing $C^\infty$-diffeomorphism $a:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ whose only fixed points are $-1,0,1$, satisfying \[ a(-1)=-1,\quad a'(-1)=\lambda_1,\qquad a(0)=0,\quad a'(0)=1/\lambda_1,\qquad a(1)=1,\quad a'(1)=\lambda_1. \]
nodes.section: 3.2 Discontinuous splittings and varying index: products of Morse-Smale maps

nodes.name: Derivative bounds on $a$
nodes.statement: Assume that, for some $\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)$ and $M>0$, \begin{equation} \lambda_1\leq a'(x)\leq\frac1{\lambda_1}, \qquad |a''(x)|\leq M, \end{equation} \[ a'(x)\leq\lambda_2 \quad\text{for }x\in(-\infty,-1+\varepsilon)\cup(1-\varepsilon,+\infty), \qquad a'(x)\geq\frac1{\lambda_2} \quad\text{for }x\in(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon). \]
nodes.section: 3.2 Discontinuous splittings and varying index: products of Morse-Smale maps

nodes.name: Derivative bounds on a (19)
nodes.statement: \lambda_1\leq a'(x)\leq\frac1{\lambda_1}, \qquad |a''(x)|\leq M,

nodes.name: Argument for generalized hyperbolicity of $a$
nodes.statement: The points $\pm 1$ are hyperbolic attracting fixed points; the point $x = 0$ is a hyperbolic repelling fixed point. For large enough~$n_0(\varepsilon)$, each trajectory $\{x_n\}$ spends at most $n_0$ steps outside $(-\infty, -1+\varepsilon) \cup (-\varepsilon, \varepsilon) \cup (1-\varepsilon, +\infty)$.
nodes.section: 3.2 Discontinuous splittings and varying index: products of Morse-Smale maps
nodes.statement_short: Orbits spend at most n_0 steps away from the attracting and repelling regions, giving uniform exponential estimates.

nodes.name: The Morse–Smale map $a$ is generalized hyperbolic
nodes.statement: Then $a$ satisfies generalized hyperbolicity with constants $C = (\lambda_1\lambda_2)^{-n_0}$, $\lambda = \lambda_2$ and splitting $$ G^s_x = \begin{cases} \mathbb{R}, \quad |x| > 1/2,\\ 0, \quad |x| \leq 1/2, \end{cases} \quad G^u_x = \begin{cases} 0, \quad |x| > 1/2,\\ \mathbb{R}, \quad |x| \leq 1/2. \end{cases} $$

conclusions: Then $a$ satisfies generalized hyperbolicity with constants $C = (\lambda_1\lambda_2)^{-n_0}$, $\lambda = \lambda_2$ and splitting

nodes.name: Infinite product of Morse–Smale maps
nodes.statement: Consider $f:\mathbb{B} \to \mathbb{B}$ defined by $ f(\{x_k\}) = \{a(x_k)\}. $ Then $f \in \mathfrak{D}(\mathbb{B})$ and satisfies generalized hyperbolicity.
nodes.section: 3.2 Discontinuous splittings and varying index: products of Morse-Smale maps
nodes.label: ex:product

nodes.name: Product map is in $\mathfrak{D}$ and generalized hyperbolic
nodes.statement: Then $f \in \mathfrak{D}(\mathbb{B})$ and satisfies generalized hyperbolicity.
nodes.section: 3.2 Discontinuous splittings and varying index: products of Morse-Smale maps
conclusions: Then $f \in \mathfrak{D}(\mathbb{B})$ and satisfies generalized hyperbolicity.

nodes.name: Proof for the product of Morse–Smale maps
nodes.statement: By \eqref{eq:aLip}, the map $a$ satisfies \eqref{eq:C1-2} with $R = 1/\lambda_1$ and \eqref{eq:C1-r1} with $r(t) = Mt$, and this $r$ satisfies \eqref{eq:C1-r2}; hence $a \in \mathfrak{D}(\mathbb{R})$. As explained above, $a$ satisfies generalized hyperbolicity with constants $C = (\lambda_1\lambda_2)^{-n_0}$, $\lambda = \lambda_2$ and the splitting $\mathbb{R} = G^s_x \oplus G^u_x$. Since $a(0) = 0$ and $$ \mathbb{B} = \ell^p(\mathbb{Z}) = \Bigl(\bigoplus_{k \in \mathbb{Z}} \mathbb{R}\Bigr)_{\ell^p}, $$ Proposition~\ref{stat:difconj}\,{\rm(P4)}, applied with $\mathbb{B}_k = \mathbb{R}$ and $f_k = a$ for every $k \in \mathbb{Z}$, shows that $f \in \mathfrak{D}(\mathbb{B})$, that $Df(\{x_k\})\{v_k\} = \{a'(x_k)v_k\}$, and that $f$ satisfies generalized hyperbolicity with the same constants $C$ and $\lambda$, with respect to the splitting $$ E^s_x = \bigoplus_{k \in \mathbb{Z}} G_{x_k}^s = \{v_k = 0, \mbox{if $|x_k| \leq 1/2$}\}, \qquad E^u_x = \bigoplus_{k \in \mathbb{Z}} G_{x_k}^u = \{v_k = 0, \mbox{if $|x_k| > 1/2$}\} $$ and the corresponding projections $P_x$, $Q_x$.
nodes.section: 3.2 Discontinuous splittings and varying index: products of Morse-Smale maps
nodes.statement_short: Show a is in D(R) and GH, then apply Proposition (P4) to the l^p product.

nodes.name: Stable index nondecreasing along trajectories
nodes.statement: The inclusion in {\rm(GH2)} has a simple dynamical interpretation in this example. Define $ I^s(x):=\{k\in\mathbb{Z}:\ |x_k|>1/2\}. $ Then $ I^s(x)\subseteq I^s(f(x)). $ Thus the stable subspace can acquire new coordinate directions along a forward trajectory. A direction is added precisely when the corresponding coordinate leaves the central repelling region and enters one of the attracting regions. In this sense, the stable index is nondecreasing along forward trajectories.
nodes.section: 3.2 Discontinuous splittings and varying index: products of Morse-Smale maps

nodes.name: Discontinuity of the product splitting
nodes.statement: The discontinuity of the splitting is visible already in one coordinate. Let $ x=\frac12e_0, $ and $x^{(m)}=\left(\frac12+\frac1m\right)e_0$. Then $x^{(m)}\to x$ in $\mathbb{B}$, whereas $ P_xe_0=0,$ $P_{x^{(m)}}e_0=e_0$. Consequently, $ \|P_{x^{(m)}}-P_x\|=1. $ In particular, the splitting is discontinuous in the operator-norm topology on the projections.
nodes.section: 3.2 Discontinuous splittings and varying index: products of Morse-Smale maps

nodes.name: Strict inclusion infinitely often
nodes.statement: The diffeomorphism $f$ satisfies generalized hyperbolicity for any $p \in [1, \infty]$; and one can choose a trajectory for which the inclusion $ Df(x_n)E^s_{x_n}\subset E^s_{x_{n+1}} $ is strict for infinitely many values of $n$.
nodes.section: 3.2 Discontinuous splittings and varying index: products of Morse-Smale maps

nodes.name: Fixed points of the product map depend on $p$
nodes.statement:
The structure of the set of fixed points, however, depends on the value of $p$. The point $\{0\} \in \mathbb{B}$ is an unstable fixed point with $E^u_{\{0\}} = \mathbb{B}$. 	extbf{Case $p \in [1, \infty)$.} A point $q = \{q_k\}$ is a fixed point if $q_k 
e 0$ only for finitely many indices $k \in \mathbb{Z}$ and for those indices $q_k = \pm 1$. For each of those points, the stable subspace $E^s_q$ is finite-dimensional with $\dim E^s_q = \#\{k: q_k 
e 0\}$. Note that the set of fixed points is countable, and each of them has a finite-dimensional stable direction; however, the dimension of the stable subspace can be arbitrarily large. 	extbf{Case $p = \infty$.} A point $q = \{q_k\} \in \mathbb{B}$ is a fixed point if $q_k \in \{-1, 0, 1\}$ for all $k \in \mathbb{Z}$. The stable subspace $E^s_q$ can be finite- or infinite-dimensional, with $\dim E^s_q=\#\{k:q_k
e0\}$, when this set is finite, and is infinite-dimensional otherwise. The number of fixed points $q$ in this case is uncountable.
nodes.section: 3.2 Discontinuous splittings and varying index: products of Morse-Smale maps
nodes.statement_short: For p<inf fixed points are countable with finite but unbounded stable dimension; for p=inf uncountably many, some with infinite-dimensional stable space.

nodes.name: Main theorem applies but Theorem SS does not
nodes.statement: For every $p\in[1,+\infty]$, all conclusions of Theorem~\ref{thm:main-results} hold for $f$. At the same time, spaces $E^s_x$, $E^u_x$ do not depend continuously on $x$, so the assumptions of Theorem~\ref{thm:SS} are not satisfied.
nodes.section: 3.2 Discontinuous splittings and varying index: products of Morse-Smale maps

nodes.name: Examples are minimal witnesses
nodes.statement: Examples~\ref{ex:shift} and~\ref{ex:product} isolate, respectively, strict invariant inclusions and a discontinuous, dimension-varying splitting. The examples are not covered by the Banach-space frameworks of \cite{SteinleinWalther1990,LaniWayda1995,Henry1981,SellYou}. That the examples are rigid is therefore the point rather than a limitation: they are minimal witnesses. Moreover, by Theorem~\ref{thm:main-results}\,(\ref{item:main-robust}) and Proposition~\ref{stat:difconj}, each generates a conjugacy-closed family that is open in the uniform $C^1$ distance within $\mathfrak{D}(\mathbb{B})$, so the phenomena they exhibit are stable, not exceptional.
nodes.section: 3.2 Discontinuous splittings and varying index: products of Morse-Smale maps
nodes.label: rem:minimal

nodes.name: North–south diffeomorphism $g$ of the circle
nodes.statement: Let $g:\mathbb{S}^1 \to \mathbb{S}^1$ be a north–south diffeomorphism of the circle.

nodes.name: Fixed points $s,u$
nodes.statement: Denote by $s, u \in \mathbb{S}^1$ its hyperbolic fixed points, where $s$ attracts and $u$ repels.

nodes.name: Weight $a$ on the circle
nodes.statement: Let $a: \mathbb{S}^1 \to \mathbb{R}^+$ be a continuous function such that \begin{equation} a(s) < 1, \quad a(u) > 1. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Weight condition at fixed points (20)
nodes.statement: a(s) < 1, \quad a(u) > 1.
nodes.label: eq:3-3-1

nodes.name: Weighted composition operator
nodes.statement: Let $\mathbb{B} = L^p(\mathbb{S}^1, \mathbb{R})$ with $p \in [1, +\infty]$, or $\mathbb{B} = C^0(\mathbb{S}^1, \mathbb{R})$. Define a linear isomorphism $T:\mathbb{B} \to \mathbb{B}$, as \begin{equation} T(v)(x) = w(x), \quad \mbox{with $w(g(x)) = a(x)v(x)$}. \end{equation} Then $T$ is generalized hyperbolic.
nodes.label: ex:coh

nodes.name: Weighted composition operator T (21)
nodes.statement: T(v)(x) = w(x), \quad \mbox{with $w(g(x)) = a(x)v(x)$}.
nodes.label: eq:3-3-T

nodes.name: Weighted composition operator is generalized hyperbolic
nodes.statement: Then $T$ is generalized hyperbolic.
conclusions: Then $T$ is generalized hyperbolic.

nodes.name: Proof for the weighted composition operator
nodes.statement: By \eqref{eq:3-3-1}, there exist $\lambda \in (0, 1)$ and interval neighborhoods $U_s$ of $s$ and $U_u$ of $u$ such that \begin{equation} g(U_s) \subset U_s, \quad a(x) < \lambda \quad x \in U_s, \end{equation} \begin{equation} g^{-1}(U_u) \subset U_u, \quad a(x) > 1/\lambda \quad x \in U_u. \end{equation} \textbf{Case 1.} $\mathbb{B} = L^p(\mathbb{S}^1, \mathbb{R})$ with $p \in [1, +\infty]$. Set $b_p(x):=a(x)|g'(x)|^{1/p}$, and set $b_\infty:=a$. Since $s$ and $u$ are hyperbolic attracting and repelling fixed points, respectively, $b_p(s)<1$, $b_p(u)>1$. For $p<+\infty$, a change of variables gives $$ |Tv|_p^p=\int_{\mathbb S^1} b_p(x)^p|v(x)|^p\,dx, $$ so $b_p$ is the effective weight for the $L^p$ estimates. Decreasing the neighborhoods $U_s,U_u$, while preserving the inclusions in \eqref{eq:3-3-s}, \eqref{eq:3-3-u}, we can assume that there exists $\lambda_p\in(0,1)$ such that $$ b_p(x)<\lambda_p\quad(x\in U_s), \qquad b_p(x)>\lambda_p^{-1}\quad(x\in U_u). $$ Let $\xi_1,\xi_2$ be the boundary points of $U_u$, set $V=\mathbb S^1\setminus U_u$, and choose $N>1$ such that $g^N(V)\subset U_s$. Define the projections $P, Q: \mathbb{B} \to \mathbb{B}$ by $$ Pv(x) = \begin{cases} v(x), & \quad x \in V, \\ 0, & \quad x \in U_u; \end{cases} \quad Qv(x) = \begin{cases} 0, & \quad x \in V, \\ v(x), & \quad x \in U_u, \end{cases} $$ and set $E^s := P(\mathbb{B})$, $E^u := Q(\mathbb{B})$. Note that \begin{equation} g(V) \subset V, \quad g^{-1}(U_u) \subset U_u, \quad V \cup U_u = \mathbb{S}^1. \end{equation} Hence $TE^s \subset E^s$, $T^{-1}E^u \subset E^u$, $P+Q = Id$. For a suitable global bound $R_p\geq1$ on $b_p$ and $b_p^{-1}$, set $C_p=(R_p/\lambda_p)^N$. The choice of $U_s,U_u,V,N$ and \eqref{eq:3-3-incl} imply that \begin{equation} |T^n v^s| \leq C_p\lambda_p^{n}|v^s|, \quad v^s \in E^s, n > 0; \end{equation} \begin{equation} |T^{-n} v^u| \leq C_p\lambda_p^{n}|v^u|, \quad v^u \in E^u, n > 0, \end{equation} and $T$ is generalized hyperbolic with the splitting $\mathbb{B} = E^s \oplus E^u$. \textbf{Case 2.} $\mathbb{B} = C^0(\mathbb{S}^1, \mathbb{R})$. For this case, take $p=+\infty$ in the preceding choice, so that $b_\infty=a$. Consider the continuous functions $ \Xi_1:[\xi_1, g(\xi_1)] \to \mathbb{R}$, $\Xi_2:[\xi_2, g(\xi_2)] \to \mathbb{R}, $ such that \begin{equation} 0 \leq \Xi_i \leq 1, \quad \Xi_1(\xi_1) = 0, \; \Xi_1(g(\xi_1)) = 1, \quad \Xi_2(\xi_2) = 0, \; \Xi_2(g(\xi_2)) = 1. \end{equation} Define the projection $P:\mathbb{B} \to \mathbb{B}$ as follows $$ Pv(x) = \begin{cases} v(x), & x \in g(V), \\ v(g(\xi_1))\Xi_1(x), & x \in [\xi_1, g(\xi_1)], \\ v(g(\xi_2))\Xi_2(x), & x \in [\xi_2, g(\xi_2)], \\ 0, & x \in U_u. \end{cases} $$ By \eqref{eq:Xi01} if $v \in \mathbb{B}$, then $Pv \in \mathbb{B}$. Define the projection $Q:\mathbb{B} \to \mathbb{B}$ by $Qv = v - Pv$. Set $E^s = P(\mathbb{B})$, $E^u = Q(\mathbb{B})$. Note that \begin{itemize} \item if $v^s \in E^s$ then $\mathrm{supp} v^s \subset V$, if $v^u \in E^u$ then $\mathrm{supp} v^u \subset \mathrm{Cl}(\mathbb{S}^1 \setminus g(V))$; \item if $\mathrm{supp} v^s \subset g(V)$ then $v^s \in E^s$, if $\mathrm{supp} v^u \subset U_u = \mathbb{S}^1 \setminus V$ then $v^u \in E^u$. \end{itemize} Hence spaces $E^s$, $E^u$ satisfy inclusions \eqref{eq:GenHypIncl}. The same argument as in Case 1, with $p=+\infty$, proves \eqref{eq:Pushs}, \eqref{eq:Pushu}. Therefore, $T$ is generalized hyperbolic.
nodes.statement_short: Choose trapping neighbourhoods of s and u, define cut-off projections (smoothly interpolated for C^0), and verify inclusions and exponential estimates.

nodes.name: Trapping neighbourhood of s (22)
nodes.statement: g(U_s) \subset U_s, \quad a(x) < \lambda \quad x \in U_s,

nodes.statement: g^{-1}(U_u) \subset U_u, \quad a(x) > 1/\lambda \quad x \in U_u.
nodes.label: eq:3-3-u

nodes.name: Invariance of V and U_u (24)
nodes.statement: g(V) \subset V, \quad g^{-1}(U_u) \subset U_u, \quad V \cup U_u = \mathbb{S}^1.
nodes.label: eq:3-3-incl

nodes.name: Stable estimate for T (25)
nodes.statement: |T^n v^s| \leq C_p\lambda_p^{n}|v^s|, \quad v^s \in E^s, n > 0;
nodes.label: eq:Pushs

nodes.name: Unstable estimate for T (26)
nodes.statement: |T^{-n} v^u| \leq C_p\lambda_p^{n}|v^u|, \quad v^u \in E^u, n > 0,
nodes.label: eq:Pushu

nodes.name: Pushforward to bounded functions
nodes.statement: Let $f \in \mathfrak{D}(\mathbb{B})$ satisfy generalized hyperbolicity. Let $X = B(\mathbb{B}, \mathbb{B})$ be the Banach space of bounded maps $\mathbb{B} \to \mathbb{B}$ with the supremum norm. Consider the linear isomorphism $T_f: X \to X$ defined as follows \begin{equation} T_fv(x) = w(x), \quad \mbox{with $w(f(x)) = Df(x)v(x)$}. \end{equation} Then $T_f$ is generalized hyperbolic.
assumptions: Let $f \in \mathfrak{D}(\mathbb{B})$ satisfy generalized hyperbolicity.
Let $X = B(\mathbb{B}, \mathbb{B})$ be the Banach space of bounded maps $\mathbb{B} \to \mathbb{B}$ with the supremum norm.
conclusions: Then $T_f$ is generalized hyperbolic.
nodes.statement_short: The pushforward T_f of a GH diffeomorphism on bounded maps B -> B is a generalized hyperbolic linear isomorphism.
nodes.label: stat:pushforward-Linfty

nodes.name: Pushforward operator T_f (28)
nodes.statement: T_fv(x) = w(x), \quad \mbox{with $w(f(x)) = Df(x)v(x)$}.
nodes.label: eq:3-3-Tf

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition (pushforward)
nodes.statement: Inequalities \eqref{eq:C1-2} imply that $T_f$ is a bounded linear isomorphism. Let $C$, $\lambda$ be the corresponding constants, and let $P_x, Q_x: \mathbb{B} \to \mathbb{B}$ be the family of projections associated with the generalized hyperbolicity of $f$. Define the projections $P, Q: X \to X$ by the following $$ Pv(x) = P_xv(x), \quad Qv(x) = Q_xv(x). $$ Condition (GH1) implies that for any $v \in X$ we have $Pv, Qv \in X$ and $|Pv|, |Qv| \leq C|v|$. Set $E^s = P(X)$, $E^u = Q(X)$. Condition (GH2) implies inclusions \eqref{eq:GenHypIncl}. Condition (GH3) implies $$ |T_f^nv^s|\leq C \lambda^n |v^s|, \quad n > 0, \; v^s \in E^s, $$ $$ |T_f^{-n}v^u|\leq C \lambda^n |v^u|, \quad n > 0, \; v^u \in E^u. $$ Therefore $T_f$ is generalized hyperbolic.
nodes.statement_short: Use the pointwise projections P_x,Q_x on X; (GH1)-(GH3) for f give the corresponding properties for T_f.

nodes.name: Regularity obstruction for other function spaces
nodes.statement: The pointwise construction in Proposition~\ref{stat:pushforward-Linfty} formally extends to other function spaces. On $X=C_b^0(\mathbb{B},\mathbb{B})$, however, the projections $Pv(x)=P_xv(x)$ and $Qv(x)=Q_xv(x)$ need not preserve continuity, while on $X=L^p(\mathbb{B},\mathbb{B})$ the same construction requires measurability of $x\mapsto P_x,Q_x$. Neither property is assumed. Thus the obstruction is regularity of the induced projections rather than the exponential estimates.

nodes.name: Diffeomorphism $h$ of a compact manifold and space of vector fields
nodes.statement: Let $h:M\to M$ be a diffeomorphism of a smooth compact manifold, and let $\mathbb{B}$ be either $L^p(M,TM)$, $p\in[1,+\infty]$, or $C_b^0(M,TM)$.

nodes.name: Pushforward operator $S_h$
nodes.statement: Define $S_h:\mathbb{B}\to\mathbb{B}$ by \begin{equation} S_h(v)(x) = w(x), \quad \mbox{with $w(h(x)) = Dh(x)v(x)$}. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Pushforward of vector fields S_h (29)
nodes.statement: S_h(v)(x) = w(x), \quad \mbox{with $w(h(x)) = Dh(x)v(x)$}.
nodes.label: eq:3-3-S

nodes.name: Mather operator
nodes.statement: When $\mathbb{B}=C_b^0(M,TM)=C^0(M,TM)$, the operator $S_h$ is the classical Mather operator associated with $h$.

nodes.name: Mather's theorem
nodes.statement: Mather proved that $h$ is Anosov if and only if $S_h$ is a hyperbolic linear operator on $C^0(M,TM)$ \cite{Mather1968}.
conclusions: $h$ is Anosov if and only if $S_h$ is a hyperbolic linear operator on $C^0(M,TM)$
equivalent_conditions: $S_h$ is a hyperbolic linear operator on $C^0(M,TM)$

nodes.name: Mather operator of an Axiom A map is generalized hyperbolic
nodes.statement: If $h$ satisfies Axiom A and the strong transversality condition, then $S_h$ is generalized hyperbolic as a linear operator on $\mathbb{B} = L^p(M, TM)$ for $p \in [1, + \infty]$, and also on $\mathbb{B} = C^0_b(M, TM)$.
assumptions: If $h$ satisfies Axiom A and the strong transversality condition
conclusions: $S_h$ is generalized hyperbolic as a linear operator on $\mathbb{B} = L^p(M, TM)$ for $p \in [1, + \infty]$, and also on $\mathbb{B} = C^0_b(M, TM)$
nodes.label: conj:AA

nodes.name: Mather operator of a north-south map is generalized hyperbolic
nodes.statement: If $h$ is a north-south diffeomorphism, an argument similar to that in Example~\ref{ex:coh} shows that $S_h$ is generalized hyperbolic.
assumptions: If $h$ is a north-south diffeomorphism
conclusions: $S_h$ is generalized hyperbolic

nodes.name: What remains for Conjecture (Axiom A)
nodes.statement: More generally, Theorem~\ref{stat:finite-dimensional-characterization} provides the pointwise splittings and exponential estimates required in Conjecture~\ref{conj:AA}, so what remains is precisely the regularity obstruction described above, now for the projections induced on a space of vector fields.

nodes.name: Sketch: finite Lipschitz shadowing by induction
nodes.statement: The proof is by induction on the length of a pseudotrajectory. Assuming that shadowing has been constructed on $[-N,N]$, we use the strong bounded solution property for the differentials $B_k=Df(y_k)$ to extend it to $[-(N+1),N+1]$.
nodes.section: 4 Scheme of the proofs of main results
nodes.statement_short: Induction on the length of the pseudotrajectory, extending shadowing from [-N,N] to [-(N+1),N+1] via the strong bounded solution property.

nodes.name: Sketch: Lipschitz shadowing in three steps
nodes.statement: The proof of Lipschitz shadowing has three main steps. \begin{enumerate} \item Lemmas \ref{lem:SBS-robust} and \ref{lem:FinLipSh} imply that the differentials $B_k=Df(y_k)$ along every sufficiently accurate finite pseudotrajectory satisfy the bounded solution property with constant~$2L$. \item Lemma~\ref{lem:Bk-Inf} extends this property to pseudotrajectories indexed by $\mathbb{Z}$, with constant $4L$. \item Lemma~\ref{lem:BS-SH} uses this bounded solvability to construct successively more accurate pseudotrajectories at summable distances from one another. Their limit is an exact trajectory shadowing the original pseudotrajectory. \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 4 Scheme of the proofs of main results
nodes.statement_short: Bounded solution property along finite pseudotrajectories, extension to Z, then successive corrections converging to an exact shadowing trajectory.

nodes.name: Sketch: periodic shadowing, density and robustness
nodes.statement: For a periodic pseudotrajectory, Lipschitz shadowing and Lemma~\ref{lem:CL-robust-Ak} imply generalized hyperbolicity of the periodic sequence of differentials, although its splitting need not be periodic. Lemma~\ref{lem:SBS-periodic} then gives the periodic bounded solution property, and the same correction procedure yields periodic shadowing. Density of periodic points in the chain-recurrent set follows from periodic shadowing, while robustness follows from the shadowing results and Lemma~\ref{lem:CL-robust-Ak} on robustness of generalized hyperbolicity for sequences of operators.
nodes.section: 4 Scheme of the proofs of main results
nodes.statement_short: Robustness gives GH of periodic differentials, periodic bounded solutions give periodic shadowing; density and robustness follow.

nodes.name: Sketch: structural stability via cocycles
nodes.statement: For Theorem~\ref{thm:SS}, we introduce generalized hyperbolicity for cocycles and construct an inverse operator analogous to that arising from the strong bounded solution property (Lemma~\ref{lem:SS1}). A Grobman--Hartman-type argument produces one semi-conjugacy, while robustness of generalized hyperbolicity for cocycles produces the reverse one (Lemma~\ref{lem:SS2}). The semi-conjugacies are constructed as near-identity maps whose corrections take values in $E_x^s\oplus F_x$. If these subspaces are independent of $x$, the admissible corrections remain in the same space under composition, and uniqueness for the corresponding conjugacy equations implies that the two semi-conjugacies are inverse to each other.
nodes.section: 4 Scheme of the proofs of main results
nodes.statement_short: Cocycle GH gives a bounded inverse; Grobman-Hartman-type and robustness arguments give two semi-conjugacies, inverse when E^s+F is constant.

nodes.name: Bounded solution property
nodes.statement: We say that a sequence of operators $\mathcal{A} = \{A_{k\in I}:\mathbb{B} \to \mathbb{B}\}$ ($I$ as in \eqref{eq:I}) with uniformly bounded norms $\|A_k\|, \|A_k^{-1}\| \leq R$ satisfies the \textit{bounded solution property on interval $I$ with constant $L>0$} if for any sequence $\{w_{k+1} \in \mathbb{B}\}_{k \in \tilde{I}}$ with $|w_{k+1}| \leq 1$ there exists a sequence $\{v_k \in \mathbb{B}\}_{k \in I}$ with $|v_k| \leq L$ such that \begin{equation} v_{k+1} = A_k v_k + w_{k+1}, \quad k \in \tilde{I}. \end{equation} If $I = \mathbb{Z}$ we say that $\mathcal{A}$ satisfies the \textit{bounded solution property with constant $L>0$}.
nodes.statement_short: Every bounded forcing {w_k} admits a solution of v_{k+1}=A_k v_k + w_{k+1} bounded by L.
nodes.label: def:bs

nodes.name: Inhomogeneous linear equation (30)
nodes.statement: v_{k+1} = A_k v_k + w_{k+1}, \quad k \in \tilde{I}.
nodes.label: eq:Inh

nodes.name: Inhomogeneous linear equations
nodes.statement: Equations \eqref{eq:Inh} are called \textit{inhomogeneous linear equations} \cite{Pli77, Coppel, Maizel1954, Palmer1984, Palmer1988, Slyusarchuk1983, ChiconeLatushkin1999, LRS-JDDE1998} and have been widely used in studies of the shadowing property \cite{Palmer2000, TikhLipSh, TikhHolSh, TikhPerSh, TikhZapSem, MonTikh, PriezzhevsTikh, Pilyugin2010, Todorov2013, Palmer1984, Palmer1988DR, BackesDragicevic2021, BD2019, BD2022}.

nodes.name: Difference operator $T_{\mathcal{A}}$
nodes.statement: The bounded solution property implies the surjectivity of the operator $T_{\mathcal{A}}: \ell^{\infty}(I, \mathbb{B}) \to \ell^{\infty}(\tilde{I}, \mathbb{B})$ defined by: \begin{equation} T_{\mathcal{A}}\{v_k\}_{k \in I} = \{v_{k+1}-A_kv_k\}_{k \in \tilde{I}}. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Difference operator T_A (31)
nodes.statement: T_{\mathcal{A}}\{v_k\}_{k \in I} = \{v_{k+1}-A_kv_k\}_{k \in \tilde{I}}.
nodes.label: eq:TA

nodes.name: Strong bounded solution property
nodes.statement: If there exists a bounded linear right inverse $S_{\mathcal{A}}$ of the operator $T_{\mathcal{A}}$ defined by \eqref{eq:TA} with $I$ defined in \eqref{eq:I} and $\|S_{\mathcal{A}}\| \leq L$, we say that $\mathcal{A}$ has the \textit{strong bounded solution property on interval $I$ with constant $L > 0$}.
differentia: a bounded linear right inverse $S_{\mathcal{A}}$ of the operator $T_{\mathcal{A}}$
nodes.label: def:sbs

nodes.name: Two-sided sequence of isomorphisms $\mathcal{A}$
nodes.statement: Consider a two-sided sequence of bounded linear isomorphisms. $$ \mathcal{A}=\{A_k: \mathbb{B} \to \mathbb{B}\}_{k\in\mathbb Z}, \qquad \|A_k\|,\;\|A_k^{-1}\|\le R. $$

nodes.name: Associated cocycle $\Phi_A$
nodes.statement: Denote the associated cocycle by $$ \Phi_A(k,\ell)=\begin{cases} A_{k-1}\dots A_{\ell} & (\ell<k),\\[2pt] I & (\ell=k),\\[2pt] A_k^{-1}\dots A_{\ell-1}^{-1} & (\ell>k). \end{cases} $$

nodes.name: Exponential dichotomy
nodes.statement: We say that the sequence $\mathcal{A}$ admits an \emph{exponential dichotomy} on $I$, where $I \in \{\mathbb{Z}^+, \mathbb{Z}^-, \mathbb{Z}\}$, if there exist constants $C>0$, $\lambda\in(0,1)$ and families of bounded projections $P_k,Q_k:\mathbb{B} \to \mathbb{B}$ ($k\in\mathbb Z$), satisfying the following properties. Denote $E^s_k:=P_k(\mathbb{B})$, $E^u_k:=Q_k(\mathbb{B})$. \begin{enumerate} \item[(ED1)] \textbf{Splitting.} $P_k+Q_k=Id$, $\|P_k\|,\|Q_k\|\le C$, hence $ E^s_k\oplus E^u_k = \mathbb{B} $. \item[(ED2)] \textbf{Invariance.} The splitting is carried exactly onto itself: $A_kE^s_k=E^s_{k+1}$, $A_k^{-1}E^u_{k+1}=E^u_{k}$ for $k\in I$. Equivalently $A_kP_k=P_{k+1}A_k$ and $A_kQ_k=Q_{k+1}A_k$. \item[(ED3)] \textbf{Exponential estimates.} For $n \geq 0$ the following estimates hold \begin{align*} &\|\Phi_A(k+n, k) v^s\|\le C\lambda^n\|v^s\|, && v^s\in E^s_k, \; [k, k+n] \subset I, \\ &\|\Phi_A(k-n, k) v^u\|\le C\lambda^n\|v^u\|, && v^u\in E^u_k, \; [k-n, k] \subset I . \end{align*} \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Bounded projections with exactly invariant splitting and uniform exponential contraction forward on E^s and backward on E^u.
nodes.label: def:exp-dichotomy

nodes.name: Transversality condition
nodes.statement: Assume that the restrictions of the sequence $\mathcal{A}$ to the future and to the past, $ {\mathcal{A}}^{+}:=\{A_k\}_{k\ge 0}, {\mathcal{A}}^{-}:=\{A_k\}_{k\le 0}, $ each admit an exponential dichotomy with splittings $E^{s,+}_k\oplus E^{u,+}_k=\mathbb{B}$ and $E^{s,-}_k\oplus E^{u,-}_k=\mathbb{B}$, respectively. We say that $\mathcal{A}$ satisfies the \emph{transversality condition} if $ E^{s,+}_0\ + E^{u,-}_0 = \mathbb{B}. $
nodes.label: def:transversality

nodes.name: Pliss–Coppel characterization of bounded right inverse
nodes.statement: In finite dimensions, an exponential dichotomy on $\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}$ and $\mathbb Z_{\le 0}$ together with the transversality condition is equivalent to the existence of a bounded (hence continuous) right inverse of the inhomogeneous difference operator $T_{\cal A}\colon\ell^\infty(\mathbb Z,\mathbb{B})\to\ell^\infty(\mathbb Z,\mathbb{B})$, $T_{\cal A}\{v_k\}=\{v_{k+1}-A_k v_k\}$, as proved in~\cite{Pli77, Coppel}.
assumptions: In finite dimensions
conclusions: an exponential dichotomy on $\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}$ and $\mathbb Z_{\le 0}$ together with the transversality condition is equivalent to the existence of a bounded (hence continuous) right inverse of the inhomogeneous difference operator
equivalent_conditions: an exponential dichotomy on $\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}$ and $\mathbb Z_{\le 0}$ together with the transversality condition
the existence of a bounded (hence continuous) right inverse of the inhomogeneous difference operator

nodes.name: Generalized hyperbolicity for sequences of operators
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{A} = \{A_k: \mathbb{B} \to \mathbb{B}\}_{k \in \mathbb{Z}}$ be a sequence of isomorphisms satisfying $\|A_k\|, \|A^{-1}_k\| \leq R$ for some $R>0$. We say that $\mathcal{A}$ satisfies \textit{generalized hyperbolicity} if there exist $C > 0$, $\lambda \in (0, 1)$ and families of projections $P_k, Q_k: \mathbb{B} \to \mathbb{B}$ satisfying the following properties. Denote $E^s_k = P_k(\mathbb{B})$, $E^u_k = Q_k(\mathbb{B})$. For every $k \in \mathbb{Z}$ the following holds \begin{itemize} \item[(GH1*)] \textbf{Splitting.} $P_k + Q_k = Id$, $\|P_k\|, \|Q_k\| \leq C$. Note that $E^s_k \oplus E^u_k = \mathbb{B}$. \item[(GH2*)] \textbf{Inclusion.} The spaces $E^s_k$ and $E^u_k$ are forward- and backward-invariant, respectively\footnote{Compare with condition (ED2), the only difference is inclusion instead of equality.} $$ A_kE^s_k \subseteq E^s_{k+1}, \quad A_k^{-1}E^u_{k+1} \subseteq E^u_{k}. $$ \item[(GH3*)] \textbf{Exponential estimates.} For every $n\ge 0$ \begin{align*} &\|\Phi_A(k+n, k) v^s\|\le C\lambda^n\|v^s\|, && v^s\in E^s_k, \\ &\|\Phi_A(k-n, k) v^u\|\le C\lambda^n\|v^u\|, && v^u\in E^u_k. \end{align*} \end{itemize} For a periodic sequence of operators with period $m$ (i.e. $A_{k+m} = A_k$), we say that $\mathcal{A}$ satisfies \textit{periodic generalized hyperbolicity} if projections $P_k$, $Q_k$ are also $m$-periodic, that is, $P_{k+m} = P_k$, $Q_{k+m} = Q_k$.
nodes.statement_short: A sequence A_k has GH if bounded projections P_k,Q_k give A_k E^s_k in E^s_{k+1}, A_k^{-1}E^u_{k+1} in E^u_k and uniform exponential estimates; periodic if P_k,Q_k are m-periodic.
nodes.label: def:CLAk

nodes.name: Orbitwise characterization
nodes.statement: Let $f \in \mathfrak{D}(\mathbb{B})$, $C > 0$, $\lambda \in (0,1)$. Then $f$ satisfies generalized hyperbolicity with constants $C, \lambda$ if and only if \begin{itemize} \item for every nonperiodic trajectory $\{x_k\}_{k \in \mathbb{Z}}$ of $f$, the sequence $\{Df(x_k)\}_{k \in \mathbb{Z}}$ satisfies generalized hyperbolicity with constants $C, \lambda$; \item for every $m$-periodic trajectory $\{x_k\}_{k \in \mathbb{Z}}$ of $f$, the sequence $\{Df(x_k)\}_{k \in \mathbb{Z}}$ satisfies $m$-periodic generalized hyperbolicity with constants $C, \lambda$. \end{itemize}
assumptions: Let $f \in \mathfrak{D}(\mathbb{B})$, $C > 0$, $\lambda \in (0,1)$.
conclusions: Then $f$ satisfies generalized hyperbolicity with constants $C, \lambda$ if and only if
equivalent_conditions: for every nonperiodic trajectory $\{x_k\}_{k \in \mathbb{Z}}$ of $f$, the sequence
nodes.statement_short: f is GH iff the derivative sequences along all trajectories are GH (periodically along periodic orbits) with the same constants.
nodes.label: lem:orbitwise

nodes.name: Proof of the orbitwise characterization
nodes.statement: If $f$ satisfies generalized hyperbolicity, set $E^{s,u}_k := E^{s,u}_{x_k}$. Then {\rm(GH1*)}--{\rm(GH3*)} are {\rm(GH1)}--{\rm(GH3)} at the points $x_k$, and if $x_{k+m} = x_k$ the splitting is automatically $m$-periodic. Conversely, the trajectories of $f$ partition $\mathbb{B}$. Choose a point $y_\omega$ in each trajectory $\omega$ and let $\{E^s_k, E^u_k\}$ be a splitting as in the hypothesis for the sequence $\{Df(f^k(y_\omega))\}$. The definition $E^{s,u}_{f^k(y_\omega)} := E^{s,u}_k$ is unambiguous: for a nonperiodic $\omega$ the points $f^k(y_\omega)$ are pairwise distinct, and for an $m$-periodic $\omega$ this is exactly the $m$-periodicity of the splitting. Conditions {\rm(GH1)}--{\rm(GH3)} then hold with constants $C, \lambda$.
nodes.statement_short: Restrict the splitting to orbits; conversely choose one base point per orbit and transport the sequence splitting (choice).

nodes.name: Pilyugin's $(C,\lambda)$-structure equivalence in finite dimensions
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{A}$ be as in Definition~\ref{def:CLAk}. Suppose $\mathcal{A}$ admits exponential dichotomies on $\mathbb{Z}^+$ and on $\mathbb{Z}^-$ and satisfies the transversality condition. In finite dimensions this implies that $\mathcal{A}$ satisfies generalized hyperbolicity; in fact, the two notions coincide, this being the $(C,\lambda)$-structure of \cite{PilCL}.
also_stated_at: At the level of sequences of linear operators, generalized hyperbolicity is equivalent in finite dimensions to exponential dichotomies on $\mathbb{Z}^\pm$ together with transversality.

For finite-dimensional sequences of linear isomorphisms, generalized hyperbolicity coincides with the existence of exponential dichotomies on $\mathbb{Z}^+$ and $\mathbb{Z}^-$ together with the transversality condition \cite{PilCL,Pli77}.
assumptions: Suppose $\mathcal{A}$ admits exponential dichotomies on $\mathbb{Z}^+$ and on $\mathbb{Z}^-$ and satisfies the transversality condition.
conclusions: In finite dimensions this implies that $\mathcal{A}$ satisfies generalized hyperbolicity; in fact, the two notions coincide

nodes.name: Generalized hyperbolicity strictly weaker in infinite dimensions
nodes.statement: In infinite dimensions, the forward implication is considerably more delicate and, unlike the finite-dimensional case, is not a routine adaptation of the classical argument; we return to it in Section~\ref{sec:discussion}. We do not use this direction in the proofs. In infinite dimensions the two notions no longer coincide: generalized hyperbolicity is strictly weaker, since the sequence of Example~\ref{ex:CL-not-ED} satisfies generalized hyperbolicity but admits no exponential dichotomy on either $\mathbb{Z}^+$ or $\mathbb{Z}^-$.

nodes.name: Strong bounded solution property along trajectories
nodes.statement: If $f \in \mathfrak{D}(\mathbb{B})$ satisfies generalized hyperbolicity, then there exists $L>0$ such that, for any exact trajectory $\{x_k\}$ and interval $I$ (finite or infinite), the associated sequence of linear operators $\mathcal{A} = \{A_k = Df(x_k)\}_{k \in I}$ satisfies the strong bounded solution property on $I$ with constant $L$.
assumptions: If $f \in \mathfrak{D}(\mathbb{B})$ satisfies generalized hyperbolicity
conclusions: there exists $L>0$ such that, for any exact trajectory $\{x_k\}$ and interval $I$ (finite or infinite), the associated sequence of linear operators $\mathcal{A} = \{A_k = Df(x_k)\}_{k \in I}$ satisfies the strong bounded solution property on $I$ with constant $L$
nodes.label: lem:SBS

nodes.name: Robustness of the bounded solution property
nodes.statement: For any $L > 0$ there exists $\varepsilon > 0$ such that the following holds. Let $I$ be an interval (finite or infinite), and let $\mathcal{A} = \{A_k\}_{k \in I}$ be a sequence satisfying the strong bounded solution property on $I$ with constant $L$. If $\mathcal{B} = \{B_k\}$ is another sequence of uniformly bounded isomorphisms satisfying $\|B_k - A_k\| \leq \varepsilon$, then it satisfies the bounded solution property on $I$ with constant~$2L$.
assumptions: let $\mathcal{A} = \{A_k\}_{k \in I}$ be a sequence satisfying the strong bounded solution property on $I$ with constant $L$
If $\mathcal{B} = \{B_k\}$ is another sequence of uniformly bounded isomorphisms satisfying

nodes.name: From finite to infinite bounded solutions
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal A=\{A_k\}_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}$ be a sequence of linear isomorphisms such that $\|A_k\|,\|A_k^{-1}\|\leq R$. Assume that there exists $L>0$ such that for any finite interval $I = (a, b)$ the sequence $\{A_k\}_{k \in I}$ satisfies the bounded solution property on $I$ with constant $L$. Then the complete sequence $\{A_k\}_{k \in \mathbb{Z}}$ satisfies the bounded solution property on $\mathbb{Z}$ with the constant $2L$.
assumptions: Let $\mathcal A=\{A_k\}_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}$ be a sequence of linear isomorphisms such that $\|A_k\|,\|A_k^{-1}\|\leq R$.
Assume that there exists $L>0$ such that for any finite interval $I = (a, b)$ the sequence $\{A_k\}_{k \in I}$ satisfies the bounded solution property on $I$ with constant $L$.
conclusions: Then the complete sequence $\{A_k\}_{k \in \mathbb{Z}}$ satisfies the bounded solution property on $\mathbb{Z}$ with the constant $2L$.
nodes.label: lem:Bk-Inf

nodes.name: Periodic bounded solutions
nodes.statement: Assume that $\mathcal{A} = \{A_k\}_{k \in \mathbb{Z}}$ is $m$-periodic ($A_{k+m}=A_k$, $k \in \mathbb{Z}$) and satisfies generalized hyperbolicity with constants $C, \lambda$, with a not necessarily periodic splitting. Then there exists $L = L(C, \lambda)>0$ such that for every bounded $m$-periodic sequence $w=\{w_k\}_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}\subset\mathbb{B}$ with $|w_k| \leq 1$ there exists an $m$-periodic sequence $v=\{v_k\}_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}\subset\mathbb{B}$, satisfying \begin{equation} v_{k+1}=A_k v_k + w_{k+1}, \quad |v_k| \leq L \qquad k\in\mathbb{Z}. \end{equation}
assumptions: Assume that $\mathcal{A} = \{A_k\}_{k \in \mathbb{Z}}$ is $m$-periodic ($A_{k+m}=A_k$, $k \in \mathbb{Z}$) and satisfies generalized hyperbolicity with constants $C, \lambda$, with a not necessarily periodic splitting.
conclusions: Then there exists $L = L(C, \lambda)>0$ such that for every bounded $m$-periodic sequence
nodes.statement_short: An m-periodic GH sequence (splitting possibly nonperiodic) admits m-periodic bounded solutions of the inhomogeneous equation.
nodes.label: lem:SBS-periodic

nodes.name: Periodic inhomogeneous equation (32)
nodes.statement: v_{k+1}=A_k v_k + w_{k+1}, \quad |v_k| \leq L \qquad k\in\mathbb{Z}.
nodes.label: eq:inhom-diff

nodes.name: Robustness of generalized hyperbolicity for sequences
nodes.statement: Assume that $\mathcal{A}=\{A_k\}$ satisfies generalized hyperbolicity with constants $C>0$, $\lambda\in(0,1)$ and $\|A_k\|,\|A_k^{-1}\|\leq R$, for $k\in\mathbb{Z}$. Then for any $\lambda_1 \in (\lambda, 1)$, there exist $C_1 = C_1(C, \lambda, \lambda_1, R)$ and $\varepsilon > 0$ such that \begin{itemize} \item[(Robust1)] any sequence $\mathcal{B} = \{B_k\}_{k \in \mathbb{Z}}$, where \begin{equation} \|B_k - A_k\| < \varepsilon, \quad k \in \mathbb{Z} \end{equation} also satisfies generalized hyperbolicity with constants $C_1$, $\lambda_1$; \item [(Robust2)] if, in addition, the sequence $\mathcal{A}$ is $m$-periodic and satisfies periodic generalized hyperbolicity, then any $m$-periodic sequence $\mathcal{B} = \{B_k\}_{k \in \mathbb{Z}}$ satisfying \eqref{eq:AkBk} also satisfies periodic generalized hyperbolicity with constants $C_1$, $\lambda_1$. \end{itemize}

conclusions: also satisfies periodic generalized hyperbolicity with constants $C_1$, $\lambda_1$

nodes.statement_short: Small bounded perturbations of a GH sequence are GH with any rate lambda_1>lambda; periodicity of the splitting is preserved.
nodes.label: lem:CL-robust-Ak

nodes.name: Perturbation size (33)
nodes.statement: \|B_k - A_k\| < \varepsilon, \quad k \in \mathbb{Z}
nodes.label: eq:AkBk

nodes.name: Non-optimal constant in robustness
nodes.statement: We expect that for sufficiently small $\varepsilon$, the sequence $\mathcal{B}$ satisfies generalized hyperbolicity for any prescribed $C_1 > C$, $\lambda_1 \in (\lambda, 1)$. However, the proof of Lemma \ref{lem:CL-robust-Ak} presented in this paper does not yield an optimal control of the constant $C_1$.

nodes.name: Generalized hyperbolic sequence without exponential dichotomy
nodes.statement: Let $\mathbb{B} = \ell^p(\mathbb{Z})$, $p \in [1, \infty]$. Consider a sequence of operators $\mathcal{A} = \{A_k: \mathbb{B} \to \mathbb{B}\}_{k \in \mathbb{Z}}$ defined as $$ (A_k x)_m = \begin{cases} \dfrac{1}{2} x_m, & m \leq k, \\ 2 x_m, & m > k. \end{cases} $$ Then $\mathcal{A}$ satisfies generalized hyperbolicity, but does not admit an exponential dichotomy on $\mathbb{Z}^+$ or $\mathbb{Z}^-$.
nodes.section: 5.1 Example of a sequence of linear operators
nodes.label: ex:CL-not-ED

nodes.name: Example sequence is GH but has no exponential dichotomy
nodes.statement: Then $\mathcal{A}$ satisfies generalized hyperbolicity, but does not admit an exponential dichotomy on $\mathbb{Z}^+$ or $\mathbb{Z}^-$.
nodes.section: 5.1 Example of a sequence of linear operators
conclusions: $\mathcal{A}$ satisfies generalized hyperbolicity
does not admit an exponential dichotomy on $\mathbb{Z}^+$ or $\mathbb{Z}^-$

nodes.name: Proof for the example without exponential dichotomy
nodes.statement: Consider the projections $$ (P_k x)_m = \begin{cases} x_m, & m \leq k, \\ 0, & m > k, \end{cases} \quad (Q_k x)_m = \begin{cases} 0, & m \leq k, \\ x_m, & m > k. \end{cases} $$ A straightforward check shows that $\mathcal{A}$ satisfies generalized hyperbolicity with projections $P_k$, $Q_k$, and $C=1$, $\lambda = 1/2$. Assume that $\mathcal{A}$ admits an exponential dichotomy on $\mathbb{Z}^+$ and denote its stable subspace at zero by $\tilde E^s_0$. Then $\tilde E^s_0$ is closed and $$ \tilde E^s_0= \left\{v\in\mathbb{B}: \lim_{n\to+\infty}|\Phi_A(n,0)v|=0 \right\}. $$ Denote by $e_m$ the standard basis vectors in $\ell^p(\mathbb{Z})$ and set $ v^{(N)}=\sum_{m=1}^N2^{-m}e_m. $ Every $v^{(N)}$ has finite support and $ |\Phi_A(n,0)v^{(N)}|\to0 $ as $n\to+\infty$. Hence $v^{(N)}\in\tilde E^s_0$. Moreover, $ v^{(N)}\to v:=\sum_{m=1}^{+\infty}2^{-m}e_m $ in $\ell^p(\mathbb{Z})$ for every $p\in[1,+\infty]$. However, the $n$-th coordinate of $\Phi_A(n,0)v$ is equal to $1$, and therefore $ |\Phi_A(n,0)v|\geq1 $ for every $n>0$. Thus $v\notin\tilde E^s_0$, contradicting the closedness of $\tilde E^s_0$. Hence $\mathcal{A}$ does not admit an exponential dichotomy on $\mathbb{Z}^+$. Similarly, $\mathcal{A}$ does not admit an exponential dichotomy on $\mathbb{Z}^-$.
nodes.section: 5.1 Example of a sequence of linear operators
nodes.statement_short: Coordinate projections give GH; an ED on Z^+ would force a closed stable space, contradicted by finitely supported approximants converging to a non-decaying vector.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma (strong bounded solution property)
nodes.statement: For an interval $I$ of the form \eqref{eq:I} the operator $S_{\mathcal{A}}$ can be defined explicitly: $S_{\mathcal{A}}\{w_{k+1}\}_{\tilde{I}} = \{v_k\}_{k \in I}$, where $v_k$ is given by Perron sums \begin{equation} v_k = \sum_{i \leq k} D(f^{k-i})(x_i) P_{x_i}w_i -\sum_{i>k}D(f^{k-i})(x_i)Q_{x_i}w_i, \end{equation} with the convention that $w_i = 0$ for $i \notin I$. By construction the operator $S_{\mathcal{A}}$ is linear. Due to~(GH1),~(GH3) $$ |v_k| \leq \sum_{i \leq k} C \lambda^{k-i}C|w_i| + \sum_{i>k} C \lambda^{i-k}C|w_i| \leq C^2 \frac{1+\lambda}{1-\lambda}\|\{w_k\}\|, $$ and hence $\|S_{\mathcal{A}}\| \leq C^2 \frac{1+\lambda}{1-\lambda}$. Conditions (GH1), (GH2) imply that $\{v_k\}$ satisfies \eqref{eq:Inh} and hence $ T_{\mathcal{A}} \circ S_{\mathcal{A}} \{w_{k+1}\}_{k \in \tilde{I}} = \{w_{k+1}\}_{k \in \tilde{I}}. $
nodes.statement_short: Define the right inverse explicitly by Perron sums and bound it with (GH1),(GH3).

nodes.name: Perron sums (34)
nodes.statement: v_k = \sum_{i \leq k} D(f^{k-i})(x_i) P_{x_i}w_i -\sum_{i>k}D(f^{k-i})(x_i)Q_{x_i}w_i,
nodes.label: eq:Perron

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma (robustness of bounded solutions)
nodes.statement: Consider $\varepsilon < \frac{1}{2L}$, operator $T_{\mathcal{A}}$ and its right inverse $S_{\mathcal{A}}$: $$ T_{\mathcal{A}} \circ S_{\mathcal{A}} = Id, \quad \|S_{\mathcal{A}}\| \leq L. $$ Let $B_k = A_k + \Delta_k$, then equation $ v_{k+1} - B_kv_k = w_{k+1}$, for $k \in \tilde{I} $ is equivalent to \begin{equation} T_{\mathcal{A}}\{v_k\} - \{\Delta_k v_k\} = \{w_{k+1}\}, \quad k \in \tilde{I}. \end{equation} Consider the operator $\Delta: \ell^{\infty}(I, \mathbb{B}) \to \ell^{\infty}(\tilde{I}, \mathbb{B})$ defined by $\Delta \{v_k\}_{k \in I} = \{w'_{k+1} = \Delta_k v_k\}_{k \in \tilde{I}}$. Note that $\| \Delta \| \leq \varepsilon$. Then any solution of the following equation is also a solution of \eqref{eq:TB1} \begin{equation} \{v_k\} - S_{\mathcal{A}}\Delta \{v_k\} = S_{\mathcal{A}}\{w_{k+1}\}. \end{equation} Note that \begin{equation} \|S_{\mathcal{A}}\Delta\|\leq L\varepsilon < \frac{1}{2}. \end{equation} Then the sequence $$ \{v_k\} = (Id - S_{\mathcal{A}}\Delta)^{-1}S_{\mathcal{A}}\{w_{k+1}\}, \quad \mbox{where} \quad (Id - S_{\mathcal{A}}\Delta)^{-1} = Id +\sum_{l \geq 1} (S_{\mathcal{A}}\Delta)^l $$ is a solution of \eqref{eq:TB2}. Due to \eqref{eq:TB3} the series converges and $$ \|\{v_k\}\| \leq \left(1+\frac{\varepsilon L}{1-\varepsilon L}\right)L \|\{w_k\}\| \leq 2L. $$
nodes.statement_short: Neumann series: rewrite the perturbed equation as (Id - S_A Delta) v = S_A w with ||S_A Delta|| < 1/2.

nodes.name: Perturbed equation via T_A (35)
nodes.statement: T_{\mathcal{A}}\{v_k\} - \{\Delta_k v_k\} = \{w_{k+1}\}, \quad k \in \tilde{I}.
nodes.label: eq:TB1

nodes.name: Fixed-point form (36)
nodes.statement: \{v_k\} - S_{\mathcal{A}}\Delta \{v_k\} = S_{\mathcal{A}}\{w_{k+1}\}.
nodes.label: eq:TB2

nodes.name: Contraction bound (37)
nodes.statement: \|S_{\mathcal{A}}\Delta\|\leq L\varepsilon < \frac{1}{2}.
nodes.label: eq:TB3

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma (finite to infinite bounded solutions)
nodes.statement_short: Lift to the shift operator on l^inf(Z,B), get finite shadowing there by solving along diagonals, then apply the Bernardes-Peris finite-to-infinite theorem. The key step reads the doubly indexed system along diagonals k-n=j.

nodes.name: Bernardes–Peris finite-to-infinite shadowing theorem
nodes.statement: For any invertible continuous linear operator $T$ on any Banach space $X$, if $T$ has the finite Lipschitz shadowing property with constant $L$, then $T$ has the Lipschitz shadowing property with constant $2L$.
assumptions: For any invertible continuous linear operator $T$ on any Banach space $X$
if $T$ has the finite Lipschitz shadowing property with constant $L$
conclusions: then $T$ has the Lipschitz shadowing property with constant $2L$

nodes.name: Constant in the Bernardes–Peris theorem
nodes.statement: The statement of Theorem 1 in \cite{NilsonPeris} gives only the shadowing property without specifying the constant. However, the proof can be repeated to establish the constant $2L$. For completeness of exposition we provide the proof tracing the constant in Appendix A.
