nodes.statement: Decreasing the neighborhoods $U_s,U_u$, while preserving the inclusions in \eqref{eq:3-3-s}, \eqref{eq:3-3-u}, we can assume that there exists $\lambda_p\in(0,1)$ such that $$ b_p(x)<\lambda_p\quad(x\in U_s), \qquad b_p(x)>\lambda_p^{-1}\quad(x\in U_u). $$
nodes.statement_short: Get rate lambda_p for b_p on the neighbourhoods.

nodes.name: Cut-off projections
nodes.statement: Let $\xi_1,\xi_2$ be the boundary points of $U_u$, set $V=\mathbb S^1\setminus U_u$, and choose $N>1$ such that $g^N(V)\subset U_s$. Define the projections $P, Q: \mathbb{B} \to \mathbb{B}$ by $$ Pv(x) = \begin{cases} v(x), & \quad x \in V, \\ 0, & \quad x \in U_u; \end{cases} \quad Qv(x) = \begin{cases} 0, & \quad x \in V, \\ v(x), & \quad x \in U_u, \end{cases} $$ and set $E^s := P(\mathbb{B})$, $E^u := Q(\mathbb{B})$.
nodes.statement_short: Define V, N and the cut-off projections P, Q.

nodes.name: Invariance
nodes.statement: Note that \begin{equation} g(V) \subset V, \quad g^{-1}(U_u) \subset U_u, \quad V \cup U_u = \mathbb{S}^1. \end{equation} Hence $TE^s \subset E^s$, $T^{-1}E^u \subset E^u$, $P+Q = Id$.
nodes.statement_short: Invariance of V and U_u gives the GH inclusions.

nodes.name: Exponential estimates
nodes.statement: For a suitable global bound $R_p\geq1$ on $b_p$ and $b_p^{-1}$, set $C_p=(R_p/\lambda_p)^N$. The choice of $U_s,U_u,V,N$ and \eqref{eq:3-3-incl} imply that \begin{equation} |T^n v^s| \leq C_p\lambda_p^{n}|v^s|, \quad v^s \in E^s, n > 0; \end{equation} \begin{equation} |T^{-n} v^u| \leq C_p\lambda_p^{n}|v^u|, \quad v^u \in E^u, n > 0, \end{equation} and $T$ is generalized hyperbolic with the splitting $\mathbb{B} = E^s \oplus E^u$.
nodes.statement_short: Exponential estimates with C_p, so T is GH.

nodes.name: Case C^0
nodes.statement: \textbf{Case 2.} $\mathbb{B} = C^0(\mathbb{S}^1, \mathbb{R})$. For this case, take $p=+\infty$ in the preceding choice, so that $b_\infty=a$. Consider the continuous functions $ \Xi_1:[\xi_1, g(\xi_1)] \to \mathbb{R}$, $\Xi_2:[\xi_2, g(\xi_2)] \to \mathbb{R}, $ such that \begin{equation} 0 \leq \Xi_i \leq 1, \quad \Xi_1(\xi_1) = 0, \; \Xi_1(g(\xi_1)) = 1, \quad \Xi_2(\xi_2) = 0, \; \Xi_2(g(\xi_2)) = 1. \end{equation} Define the projection $P:\mathbb{B} \to \mathbb{B}$ as follows $$ Pv(x) = \begin{cases} v(x), & x \in g(V), \\ v(g(\xi_1))\Xi_1(x), & x \in [\xi_1, g(\xi_1)], \\ v(g(\xi_2))\Xi_2(x), & x \in [\xi_2, g(\xi_2)], \\ 0, & x \in U_u. \end{cases} $$ By \eqref{eq:Xi01} if $v \in \mathbb{B}$, then $Pv \in \mathbb{B}$. Define the projection $Q:\mathbb{B} \to \mathbb{B}$ by $Qv = v - Pv$. Set $E^s = P(\mathbb{B})$, $E^u = Q(\mathbb{B})$. Note that \begin{itemize} \item if $v^s \in E^s$ then $\mathrm{supp} v^s \subset V$, if $v^u \in E^u$ then $\mathrm{supp} v^u \subset \mathrm{Cl}(\mathbb{S}^1 \setminus g(V))$; \item if $\mathrm{supp} v^s \subset g(V)$ then $v^s \in E^s$, if $\mathrm{supp} v^u \subset U_u = \mathbb{S}^1 \setminus V$ then $v^u \in E^u$. \end{itemize} Hence spaces $E^s$, $E^u$ satisfy inclusions \eqref{eq:GenHypIncl}. The same argument as in Case 1, with $p=+\infty$, proves \eqref{eq:Pushs}, \eqref{eq:Pushu}. Therefore, $T$ is generalized hyperbolic.
nodes.statement_short: C^0 case: continuous interpolated projections.

nodes.name: Continuous cut-off
nodes.statement: \textbf{Case 2.} $\mathbb{B} = C^0(\mathbb{S}^1, \mathbb{R})$. For this case, take $p=+\infty$ in the preceding choice, so that $b_\infty=a$. Consider the continuous functions $ \Xi_1:[\xi_1, g(\xi_1)] \to \mathbb{R}$, $\Xi_2:[\xi_2, g(\xi_2)] \to \mathbb{R}, $ such that \begin{equation} 0 \leq \Xi_i \leq 1, \quad \Xi_1(\xi_1) = 0, \; \Xi_1(g(\xi_1)) = 1, \quad \Xi_2(\xi_2) = 0, \; \Xi_2(g(\xi_2)) = 1. \end{equation} Define the projection $P:\mathbb{B} \to \mathbb{B}$ as follows $$ Pv(x) = \begin{cases} v(x), & x \in g(V), \\ v(g(\xi_1))\Xi_1(x), & x \in [\xi_1, g(\xi_1)], \\ v(g(\xi_2))\Xi_2(x), & x \in [\xi_2, g(\xi_2)], \\ 0, & x \in U_u. \end{cases} $$ By \eqref{eq:Xi01} if $v \in \mathbb{B}$, then $Pv \in \mathbb{B}$. Define the projection $Q:\mathbb{B} \to \mathbb{B}$ by $Qv = v - Pv$. Set $E^s = P(\mathbb{B})$, $E^u = Q(\mathbb{B})$. Note that \begin{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Define the interpolating functions Xi_i and the continuous projections P, Q.

nodes.name: Support property 1
nodes.statement: if $v^s \in E^s$ then $\mathrm{supp} v^s \subset V$, if $v^u \in E^u$ then $\mathrm{supp} v^u \subset \mathrm{Cl}(\mathbb{S}^1 \setminus g(V))$;
nodes.statement_short: Supports of stable and unstable vectors.

nodes.name: Support property 2
nodes.statement: if $\mathrm{supp} v^s \subset g(V)$ then $v^s \in E^s$, if $\mathrm{supp} v^u \subset U_u = \mathbb{S}^1 \setminus V$ then $v^u \in E^u$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Sufficient support conditions for membership.

nodes.name: Conclude C^0 case
nodes.statement: Hence spaces $E^s$, $E^u$ satisfy inclusions \eqref{eq:GenHypIncl}. The same argument as in Case 1, with $p=+\infty$, proves \eqref{eq:Pushs}, \eqref{eq:Pushu}. Therefore, $T$ is generalized hyperbolic.
nodes.statement_short: Inclusions hold and the Case 1 estimates with p=inf give GH.

nodes.name: T_f is an isomorphism
nodes.statement: Inequalities \eqref{eq:C1-2} imply that $T_f$ is a bounded linear isomorphism.
nodes.statement_short: Derivative bounds make T_f a bounded isomorphism.

nodes.name: Pointwise projections
nodes.statement: Let $C$, $\lambda$ be the corresponding constants, and let $P_x, Q_x: \mathbb{B} \to \mathbb{B}$ be the family of projections associated with the generalized hyperbolicity of $f$. Define the projections $P, Q: X \to X$ by the following $$ Pv(x) = P_xv(x), \quad Qv(x) = Q_xv(x). $$
nodes.statement_short: Define P, Q on X pointwise from P_x, Q_x.

nodes.name: GH1 for T_f
nodes.statement: Condition (GH1) implies that for any $v \in X$ we have $Pv, Qv \in X$ and $|Pv|, |Qv| \leq C|v|$. Set $E^s = P(X)$, $E^u = Q(X)$.
nodes.statement_short: Projection bounds from (GH1).

nodes.name: GH2 for T_f
nodes.statement: Condition (GH2) implies inclusions \eqref{eq:GenHypIncl}.
nodes.statement_short: Inclusions from (GH2).

nodes.name: GH3 for T_f
nodes.statement: Condition (GH3) implies $$ |T_f^nv^s|\leq C \lambda^n |v^s|, \quad n > 0, \; v^s \in E^s, $$ $$ |T_f^{-n}v^u|\leq C \lambda^n |v^u|, \quad n > 0, \; v^u \in E^u. $$ Therefore $T_f$ is generalized hyperbolic.
nodes.statement_short: Exponential estimates from (GH3); T_f is GH.

nodes.name: Outline
nodes.statement: The proof of Lipschitz shadowing has three main steps. \begin{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Three-step outline.
nodes.section: 4 Scheme of the proofs of main results

nodes.name: Finite bounded solutions
nodes.statement: Lemmas \ref{lem:SBS-robust} and \ref{lem:FinLipSh} imply that the differentials $B_k=Df(y_k)$ along every sufficiently accurate finite pseudotrajectory satisfy the bounded solution property with constant~$2L$.
nodes.statement_short: Bounded solution property with constant 2L along finite pseudotrajectories.
nodes.section: 4 Scheme of the proofs of main results

nodes.name: Extension to Z
nodes.statement: Lemma~\ref{lem:Bk-Inf} extends this property to pseudotrajectories indexed by $\mathbb{Z}$, with constant $4L$.
nodes.statement_short: Extend to Z with constant 4L.
nodes.section: 4 Scheme of the proofs of main results

nodes.name: Successive corrections
nodes.statement: Lemma~\ref{lem:BS-SH} uses this bounded solvability to construct successively more accurate pseudotrajectories at summable distances from one another. Their limit is an exact trajectory shadowing the original pseudotrajectory. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Successive corrections converge to an exact shadowing trajectory.
nodes.section: 4 Scheme of the proofs of main results

nodes.name: Periodic shadowing
nodes.statement: For a periodic pseudotrajectory, Lipschitz shadowing and Lemma~\ref{lem:CL-robust-Ak} imply generalized hyperbolicity of the periodic sequence of differentials, although its splitting need not be periodic. Lemma~\ref{lem:SBS-periodic} then gives the periodic bounded solution property, and the same correction procedure yields periodic shadowing.
nodes.statement_short: Robustness and periodic bounded solutions give periodic shadowing.
nodes.section: 4 Scheme of the proofs of main results

nodes.name: Density and robustness
nodes.statement: Density of periodic points in the chain-recurrent set follows from periodic shadowing, while robustness follows from the shadowing results and Lemma~\ref{lem:CL-robust-Ak} on robustness of generalized hyperbolicity for sequences of operators.
nodes.statement_short: Density from periodic shadowing; robustness from shadowing and sequence robustness.
nodes.section: 4 Scheme of the proofs of main results

nodes.name: Cocycle inverse
nodes.statement: For Theorem~\ref{thm:SS}, we introduce generalized hyperbolicity for cocycles and construct an inverse operator analogous to that arising from the strong bounded solution property (Lemma~\ref{lem:SS1}).
nodes.statement_short: Cocycle GH yields a bounded inverse operator.
nodes.section: 4 Scheme of the proofs of main results

nodes.name: Two semi-conjugacies
nodes.statement: A Grobman--Hartman-type argument produces one semi-conjugacy, while robustness of generalized hyperbolicity for cocycles produces the reverse one (Lemma~\ref{lem:SS2}).
nodes.statement_short: Grobman-Hartman argument and cocycle robustness give the two semi-conjugacies.
nodes.section: 4 Scheme of the proofs of main results

nodes.name: Inverse to each other
nodes.statement: The semi-conjugacies are constructed as near-identity maps whose corrections take values in $E_x^s\oplus F_x$. If these subspaces are independent of $x$, the admissible corrections remain in the same space under composition, and uniqueness for the corresponding conjugacy equations implies that the two semi-conjugacies are inverse to each other.
nodes.statement_short: If E^s + F is constant, uniqueness makes them mutually inverse.
nodes.section: 4 Scheme of the proofs of main results

nodes.name: Forward direction
nodes.statement: If $f$ satisfies generalized hyperbolicity, set $E^{s,u}_k := E^{s,u}_{x_k}$. Then {\rm(GH1*)}--{\rm(GH3*)} are {\rm(GH1)}--{\rm(GH3)} at the points $x_k$, and if $x_{k+m} = x_k$ the splitting is automatically $m$-periodic.
nodes.statement_short: Restrict the splitting of f to the orbit.

nodes.name: Converse direction
nodes.statement: Conversely, the trajectories of $f$ partition $\mathbb{B}$. Choose a point $y_\omega$ in each trajectory $\omega$ and let $\{E^s_k, E^u_k\}$ be a splitting as in the hypothesis for the sequence $\{Df(f^k(y_\omega))\}$. The definition $E^{s,u}_{f^k(y_\omega)} := E^{s,u}_k$ is unambiguous: for a nonperiodic $\omega$ the points $f^k(y_\omega)$ are pairwise distinct, and for an $m$-periodic $\omega$ this is exactly the $m$-periodicity of the splitting. Conditions {\rm(GH1)}--{\rm(GH3)} then hold with constants $C, \lambda$.
nodes.statement_short: Choose a base point per orbit and transport the sequence splitting.

nodes.name: GH via coordinate projections
nodes.statement: Consider the projections $$ (P_k x)_m = \begin{cases} x_m, & m \leq k, \\ 0, & m > k, \end{cases} \quad (Q_k x)_m = \begin{cases} 0, & m \leq k, \\ x_m, & m > k. \end{cases} $$ A straightforward check shows that $\mathcal{A}$ satisfies generalized hyperbolicity with projections $P_k$, $Q_k$, and $C=1$, $\lambda = 1/2$.
nodes.statement_short: Coordinate projections give GH with C=1, lambda=1/2.
nodes.section: 5.1 Example of a sequence of linear operators

nodes.name: Assume ED
nodes.statement: Assume that $\mathcal{A}$ admits an exponential dichotomy on $\mathbb{Z}^+$ and denote its stable subspace at zero by $\tilde E^s_0$. Then $\tilde E^s_0$ is closed and $$ \tilde E^s_0= \left\{v\in\mathbb{B}: \lim_{n\to+\infty}|\Phi_A(n,0)v|=0 \right\}. $$
nodes.statement_short: Assume an ED on Z^+; its stable space is closed and characterized by decay.
nodes.section: 5.1 Example of a sequence of linear operators

nodes.name: Finitely supported approximants
nodes.statement: Denote by $e_m$ the standard basis vectors in $\ell^p(\mathbb{Z})$ and set $ v^{(N)}=\sum_{m=1}^N2^{-m}e_m. $ Every $v^{(N)}$ has finite support and $ |\Phi_A(n,0)v^{(N)}|\to0 $ as $n\to+\infty$. Hence $v^{(N)}\in\tilde E^s_0$.
nodes.statement_short: Finitely supported v^(N) lie in the stable space.
nodes.section: 5.1 Example of a sequence of linear operators

nodes.name: Contradiction
nodes.statement: Moreover, $ v^{(N)}\to v:=\sum_{m=1}^{+\infty}2^{-m}e_m $ in $\ell^p(\mathbb{Z})$ for every $p\in[1,+\infty]$. However, the $n$-th coordinate of $\Phi_A(n,0)v$ is equal to $1$, and therefore $ |\Phi_A(n,0)v|\geq1 $ for every $n>0$. Thus $v\notin\tilde E^s_0$, contradicting the closedness of $\tilde E^s_0$. Hence $\mathcal{A}$ does not admit an exponential dichotomy on $\mathbb{Z}^+$. Similarly, $\mathcal{A}$ does not admit an exponential dichotomy on $\mathbb{Z}^-$.
nodes.statement_short: The limit v does not decay, contradicting closedness; similarly for Z^-.
nodes.section: 5.1 Example of a sequence of linear operators

nodes.name: Perron sums
nodes.statement: For an interval $I$ of the form \eqref{eq:I} the operator $S_{\mathcal{A}}$ can be defined explicitly: $S_{\mathcal{A}}\{w_{k+1}\}_{\tilde{I}} = \{v_k\}_{k \in I}$, where $v_k$ is given by Perron sums \begin{equation} v_k = \sum_{i \leq k} D(f^{k-i})(x_i) P_{x_i}w_i -\sum_{i>k}D(f^{k-i})(x_i)Q_{x_i}w_i, \end{equation} with the convention that $w_i = 0$ for $i \notin I$. By construction the operator $S_{\mathcal{A}}$ is linear.
nodes.statement_short: Define the right inverse by Perron sums.

nodes.name: Norm bound
nodes.statement: Due to~(GH1),~(GH3) $$ |v_k| \leq \sum_{i \leq k} C \lambda^{k-i}C|w_i| + \sum_{i>k} C \lambda^{i-k}C|w_i| \leq C^2 \frac{1+\lambda}{1-\lambda}\|\{w_k\}\|, $$ and hence $\|S_{\mathcal{A}}\| \leq C^2 \frac{1+\lambda}{1-\lambda}$.
nodes.statement_short: Geometric series bound C^2(1+lambda)/(1-lambda).

nodes.name: Right inverse
nodes.statement: Conditions (GH1), (GH2) imply that $\{v_k\}$ satisfies \eqref{eq:Inh} and hence $ T_{\mathcal{A}} \circ S_{\mathcal{A}} \{w_{k+1}\}_{k \in \tilde{I}} = \{w_{k+1}\}_{k \in \tilde{I}}. $
nodes.statement_short: The Perron sums solve the inhomogeneous equation.

nodes.name: Right inverse of T_A
nodes.statement: Consider $\varepsilon < \frac{1}{2L}$, operator $T_{\mathcal{A}}$ and its right inverse $S_{\mathcal{A}}$: $$ T_{\mathcal{A}} \circ S_{\mathcal{A}} = Id, \quad \|S_{\mathcal{A}}\| \leq L. $$
nodes.statement_short: Fix epsilon < 1/(2L) and the right inverse S_A.

nodes.name: Rewrite perturbed equation
nodes.statement: Let $B_k = A_k + \Delta_k$, then equation $ v_{k+1} - B_kv_k = w_{k+1}$, for $k \in \tilde{I} $ is equivalent to \begin{equation} T_{\mathcal{A}}\{v_k\} - \{\Delta_k v_k\} = \{w_{k+1}\}, \quad k \in \tilde{I}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite the perturbed equation via T_A.

nodes.name: Perturbation operator
nodes.statement: Consider the operator $\Delta: \ell^{\infty}(I, \mathbb{B}) \to \ell^{\infty}(\tilde{I}, \mathbb{B})$ defined by $\Delta \{v_k\}_{k \in I} = \{w'_{k+1} = \Delta_k v_k\}_{k \in \tilde{I}}$. Note that $\| \Delta \| \leq \varepsilon$.
nodes.statement_short: The perturbation operator has norm at most epsilon.

nodes.name: Fixed-point form
nodes.statement: Then any solution of the following equation is also a solution of \eqref{eq:TB1} \begin{equation} \{v_k\} - S_{\mathcal{A}}\Delta \{v_k\} = S_{\mathcal{A}}\{w_{k+1}\}. \end{equation} Note that \begin{equation} \|S_{\mathcal{A}}\Delta\|\leq L\varepsilon < \frac{1}{2}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to (Id - S_A Delta)v = S_A w with ||S_A Delta|| < 1/2.

nodes.name: Neumann series
nodes.statement: Then the sequence $$ \{v_k\} = (Id - S_{\mathcal{A}}\Delta)^{-1}S_{\mathcal{A}}\{w_{k+1}\}, \quad \mbox{where} \quad (Id - S_{\mathcal{A}}\Delta)^{-1} = Id +\sum_{l \geq 1} (S_{\mathcal{A}}\Delta)^l $$ is a solution of \eqref{eq:TB2}. Due to \eqref{eq:TB3} the series converges and $$ \|\{v_k\}\| \leq \left(1+\frac{\varepsilon L}{1-\varepsilon L}\right)L \|\{w_k\}\| \leq 2L. $$
nodes.statement_short: Neumann series gives a solution bounded by 2L.

nodes.name: Bernardes-Peris theorem
nodes.statement: We use the following statement for linear isomorphisms of Banach spaces. \begin{thm}[{\cite[Theorem 1]{NilsonPeris}}] For any invertible continuous linear operator $T$ on any Banach space $X$, if $T$ has the finite Lipschitz shadowing property with constant $L$, then $T$ has the Lipschitz shadowing property with constant $2L$. \end{thm} \begin{remark} The statement of Theorem 1 in \cite{NilsonPeris} gives only the shadowing property without specifying the constant. However, the proof can be repeated to establish the constant $2L$. For completeness of exposition we provide the proof tracing the constant in Appendix A. \end{remark}
nodes.statement_short: Quote the finite-to-infinite shadowing theorem for linear operators.

nodes.name: Lifted operator
nodes.statement: Consider the Banach space$ \mathfrak{X} =\ell^{\infty}(\mathbb{Z}, \mathbb{B})=\bigl\{\{v_n\}_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}: v_n\in \mathbb{B} \bigr\} $ and a linear operator $\mathfrak{A} \colon \mathfrak{X} \to \mathfrak{X}$ defined by $$ \mathfrak{A}\{v_n\}=\{v_n'\}, \qquad \text{where }\; v_{n+1}'=A_n v_n. $$
nodes.statement_short: Introduce the shift-type operator on l^inf(Z,B).

nodes.name: Finite shadowing of the lifted operator
nodes.statement_short: Show the lifted operator has finite Lipschitz shadowing with constant L, then Lipschitz shadowing with 2L.

nodes.name: Finite data and reformulation
nodes.statement_short: Fix a finite interval and forcing, and write the lifted equations coordinatewise.

nodes.name: Diagonal variables
nodes.statement: The idea is to read the doubly-indexed system \eqref{eq:1-inf} along the diagonals $k-n=j$: on each of them it becomes a finite inhomogeneous difference equation in the single index $n$ for the operators $\{A_n\}$, to which the finite bounded solution property applies. Denote $j := k-n$ and consider the sequences \begin{equation} \mu_n^j := \nu_n^{j+n},\qquad \theta_n^j := \xi_n^{j+n-1}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Change to diagonal variables j = k - n.

nodes.name: Diagonal equations
nodes.statement: Then \eqref{eq:1-inf} is equivalent to \begin{equation} \mu_{n+1}^j = A_n\mu_n^j+\theta_{n+1}^j,\qquad n\in\mathbb{Z},\; n+j\in[k_1,k_2-1]. \end{equation} Rewriting indexes we have \begin{equation} \mu_{n+1}^j = A_n\mu_n^j+\theta_{n+1}^j,\qquad j\in\mathbb{Z},\; n\in[k_1-j,\,k_2-j-1]. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: On each diagonal obtain a finite inhomogeneous equation.

nodes.name: Solve and apply theorem
nodes.statement: For any $j\in\mathbb{Z}$, according to \eqref{eq:Inh} there exists a sequence $\mu^j_n$ satisfying \eqref{eq:2'}, and $|\mu_n^j| \le L$ for $n\in[k_1-j,k_2-j]$. Hence, for all $j\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $n+j\in[k_1,k_2-1]$, \eqref{eq:2} holds, which means that $\nu_n^k$ defined by \eqref{eq:1.5} satisfies \eqref{eq:1-inf}. Hence, the operator $\mathfrak{A}$ has the finite Lipschitz shadowing property with constant $L$. According to Theorem \ref{thm:Bernandes-shadowing}, this implies that $\mathfrak{A}$ has the Lipschitz shadowing property with constant $2L$.
nodes.statement_short: Solve each diagonal with constant L and apply the Bernardes-Peris theorem.

nodes.name: Constant forcing
nodes.statement: Let us now show that the sequence $\mathcal{A}$ satisfies the bounded solution property for $I = \mathbb{Z}$. Indeed, fix $\{w_k \in \mathbb{B}\}$ with $|w_k| \leq 1$. Consider the sequence $\xi^k \in \mathfrak{X}$ defined as $$ \xi^k = \{ \dots, w_{k+1}, w_{k+1}, w_{k+1}, \dots\}, \; \xi^k_n = w_{k+1}, \quad n\in \mathbb{Z}. $$ Note that $|\xi^k| = |w_{k+1}| \leq 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Embed the forcing as constant sequences xi^k.

nodes.name: Shadow in lifted space
nodes.statement_short: Shadowing of the lifted operator gives nu^k bounded by 2L.

nodes.name: Diagonal solution
nodes.statement:
Denote $
u^k = \{
u^k_n\}$, then $|
u^k_n| \leq 2L$. According to \eqref{eq:nu-inf}, the sequence $v_k = 
u^k_k$ satisfies \eqref{eq:Inh} for $I = \mathbb{Z}$ and hence $\mathcal{A}$ satisfies the bounded solution property with constant $2L$ for $I = \mathbb{Z}$.
nodes.statement_short: The diagonal v_k = nu^k_k solves the equation on Z with constant 2L.

nodes.name: Periodic shift identity
nodes.statement: For $i\in\mathbb{Z}$, let $r(i)\in\{0,\ldots,m-1\}$ be its residue modulo $m$. Periodicity gives $ \Phi_A(k+m,\ell+m)=\Phi_A(k,\ell) $ and, writing $i=r(i)+qm$, we have \begin{equation} \Phi_A(k,i)=\Phi_A(k-i+r(i),r(i)). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Residues and the periodicity identity for Phi_A.

nodes.name: Green-type series
nodes.statement: Consider the sequence \begin{equation} v_k:= \sum_{i \leq k}\Phi_A(k,i)P_{r(i)}w_{i} -\sum_{ i > k}\Phi_A(k,i)Q_{r(i)}w_{i}, \quad k \in \mathbb{Z}. \end{equation} Although the splitting need not be periodic, \eqref{eq:periodic-shift} allows us to use the projections at the representative indices $r(i)$.
nodes.statement_short: Define v_k by a Green series with projections at r(i).

nodes.name: Convergence and bound
nodes.statement: By \eqref{eq:periodic-shift} and {\rm(GH1*)}, {\rm(GH3*)}, \[ \|\Phi_A(k,i)P_{r(i)}\| \leq C^2\lambda^{k-i}, \qquad i\leq k, \] \[ \|\Phi_A(k,i)Q_{r(i)}\| \leq C^2\lambda^{i-k}, \qquad i>k. \] Hence the series in \eqref{eq:green-series} converge. Summing the geometric tail yields $|v_k| \leq L = C^{2}\frac{1+\lambda}{1-\lambda}$.
nodes.statement_short: Exponential bounds give convergence and |v_k| <= L.

nodes.name: Periodicity
nodes.statement: Changing the summation index by $m$ and using \[ \Phi_A(k+m,i+m)=\Phi_A(k,i),\qquad r(i+m)=r(i),\qquad w_{i+m}=w_i, \] gives $v_{k+m}=v_k$.
nodes.statement_short: Shift of index shows v is m-periodic.

nodes.name: Solves the equation
nodes.statement: Moreover, using $ A_k\Phi_A(k,i)=\Phi_A(k+1,i) $ and $P_{r(k+1)}+Q_{r(k+1)}=Id$, direct cancellation in \eqref{eq:green-series} gives $ v_{k+1}=A_kv_k+w_{k+1}. $
nodes.statement_short: Direct cancellation shows v solves the inhomogeneous equation.

nodes.name: Block decomposition
nodes.statement: Let $B_k = A_k + \Delta_k$. Denote $$ A_k = \begin{bmatrix} A_k^{ss} & A_k^{su} \\ A_k^{us} & A_k^{uu} \end{bmatrix} , \quad \Delta_k = \begin{bmatrix} \Delta_k^{ss} & \Delta_k^{su} \\ \Delta_k^{us} & \Delta_k^{uu} \end{bmatrix}, $$ where \begin{align*} A_k^{ss}: E_k^s \to E_{k+1}^s, & \quad A_k^{ss} = P_{k+1}A_k;& \qquad A_k^{su}: E_k^u \to E_{k+1}^s, & \quad A_k^{su} = P_{k+1}A_k;\\ A_k^{us}: E_k^s \to E_{k+1}^u, & \quad A_k^{us} = Q_{k+1}A_k;& \qquad A_k^{uu}: E_k^u \to E_{k+1}^u, & \quad A_k^{uu} = Q_{k+1}A_k, \end{align*} The operators $\Delta_k^{ss}$, $\Delta_k^{su}$, $\Delta_k^{us}$, and $\Delta_k^{uu}$ are defined in the same way, replacing $A_k$ by $\Delta_k$.
nodes.statement_short: Write A_k and Delta_k as block operators w.r.t. the splitting.

nodes.name: Triangular form and Z_k
nodes.statement: By (GH2*) we have $A_k^{us}=0$, and therefore $$ A_k = \begin{bmatrix} A_k^{ss} & A_k^{su} \\ 0 & A_k^{uu} \end{bmatrix} $$ Denote $ F_k^u = A_k^{-1} E_{k+1}^u. $ By (GH2*) we have $F_k^u \subseteq E_k^u$, and the map $A_k:F_k^u \to E_{k+1}^u$ is a bijection. Therefore, it has an inverse; denote it by $Z_k: E_{k+1}^u \to F_k^u$, $$ Z_kA_k^{uu} = Id|_{F_k^u}, \quad A_k^{uu}Z_k = Id|_{E_{k+1}^u}, \quad Z_k = A_k^{-1}|_{E^u_{k+1}}. $$
nodes.statement_short: GH2* makes A_k block upper triangular; define the inverse Z_k on F^u.

nodes.name: Choice of constants
nodes.statement: Let us first prove item \textit{(Robust1)}. Denote $L' = 1+ C^2 \frac{\lambda^2}{1-\lambda^2}$. Fix $\varepsilon<1/(2R)$ sufficiently small so that, for \begin{equation} \varepsilon_1 = C\varepsilon, \quad \varepsilon_2 = 2L'R\varepsilon_1 \end{equation} the following inequality holds \begin{equation} R(2\varepsilon_1 + 2(R+\varepsilon_1)\varepsilon_2 + (R+\varepsilon_1)2\varepsilon_2) \leq \frac{1}{2L'}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Fix epsilon, epsilon_1, epsilon_2 and L' so the contraction condition holds.

nodes.name: B_k invertible
nodes.statement: Since $ \|A_k^{-1}(B_k-A_k)\|<\frac{1}{2}, $ each $B_k$ is an isomorphism and $ \|B_k^{-1}\|\leq 2R. $
nodes.statement_short: B_k are isomorphisms with ||B_k^{-1}|| <= 2R.

nodes.name: Goal: invariant graphs
nodes.statement: In the following we show that there exists a sequence of linear maps $H_k: E_k^s \to F_k^u$, $\|H_k\| \leq \varepsilon_2$, such that for linear spaces \begin{equation} \tilde{E}_k^s = \{v_k^s+H_k v_k^s: \; v_k^s \in E_k^s\} \end{equation} holds the inclusion \begin{equation} B_k \tilde{E}_k^s \subseteq \tilde{E}_{k+1}^s. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Seek H_k so that the graphs of H_k are B-invariant.

nodes.name: Remark on dichotomy case
nodes.statement: \begin{remark} In the standard robustness proof for exponential dichotomy, the latter inclusion is replaced by an equality, and the operators $H_k$ are assumed to act on $E_k^u$. These differences lead to the corresponding changes in the arguments. \end{remark}
nodes.statement_short: Remark: difference with the exponential dichotomy proof.

nodes.name: Invariance equation
nodes.statement: Consider the vectors $v_k^s \in E_k^s$ and $\tilde{v}_k^s = v_k^s + H_k v_k^s \in \tilde{E}_k^s$. The following holds \begin{multline*} B_k \tilde{v}_k^s = \left(\begin{bmatrix} A_k^{ss} & A_k^{su} \\ 0 & A_k^{uu} \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} \Delta_k^{ss} & \Delta_k^{su} \\ \Delta_k^{us} & \Delta_k^{uu} \end{bmatrix} \right) \begin{bmatrix} v_k^s \\ H_k v_k^s \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} A_k^{ss}v_k^s + A_k^{su}H_kv_k^s + \Delta_{k}^{ss}v_k^s + \Delta_k^{su} H_k v_k^s \\ A_k^{uu}H_kv_k^s + \Delta_k^{us}v_k^s + \Delta_k^{uu}H_k v_k^s \end{bmatrix}. \end{multline*} Inclusion $B_k \tilde{v}_k^s \in \tilde{E}_{k+1}^s$ is equivalent to equality $$ (H_{k+1}A_k^{ss} + H_{k+1}A_k^{su}H_k + H_{k+1}\Delta_k^{ss} + H_{k+1}\Delta_k^{su}H_k)v_k^s = (A_k^{uu}H_k + \Delta_k^{us} + \Delta_k^{uu}H_k)v_k^s. $$
nodes.statement_short: Invariance of the graphs is equivalent to an operator equation for H.

nodes.name: Sufficient condition
nodes.statement: \begin{statement} If a sequence of operators $H_k: E_k^s \to F_k^u$ satisfies \begin{equation} A_k^{uu}H_k = H_{k+1}A_k^{ss} - \Delta_k^{us} - \Delta_k^{uu}H_k + H_{k+1}A_k^{su}H_k + H_{k+1}\Delta_k^{ss} + H_{k+1}\Delta_k^{su}H_k \end{equation} then inclusions \eqref{eq:ETildaIncl} hold. \end{statement}
nodes.statement_short: State the sufficient condition (Proposition) for invariance.

nodes.name: Auxiliary linear problem
nodes.statement: Consider the following auxiliary problem. Given a sequence of bounded operators $S_k: E_k^s \to F_k^u$, we seek a bounded sequence of operators $H_k: E_k^s \to F_k^u$ that satisfies \begin{equation} H_k = Z_kH_{k+1}A_k^{ss} + S_k. \end{equation} Let $X$ be the Banach space of such operator sequences $\{S_k\}_{k \in \mathbb{Z}}$ endowed with the norm $\|\{S_k\}\| = \sup_k \|S_k\|$. Consider the operator $F:X\to X$ defined by \begin{equation} F(\{S_k\}) = \{H_k\}, \quad \mbox{where} \quad H_k = S_k + \sum_{l = 1}^{+\infty}Z_k\cdot \ldots \cdot Z_{k+(l-1)}S_{k+l}A_{k+(l-1)}^{ss} \cdot \ldots \cdot A_k^{ss}. \end{equation} Due to condition (GH3*) for $l \geq 0$, the following inequalities hold $$ \|Z_k\cdot \ldots \cdot Z_{k+(l-1)}\| \leq C \lambda^l, \quad \|A_{k+(l-1)}^{ss}\cdot \ldots \cdot A_k^{ss}\| \leq C \lambda^l. $$ Hence, the right-hand side of \eqref{eq:defFHk} converges and \begin{equation} \|F(\{S_k\})\| \leq \|\{S_k\}\| \left(1+ \sum_{l=1}^{\infty} C^2\lambda^{2l} \right) = \|\{S_k\}\|\left(1+ C^2 \frac{\lambda^2}{1-\lambda^2}\right) = L' \|\{S_k\}\|. \end{equation} A straightforward substitution shows that $H_k$, $S_k$ satisfy \eqref{eq:HkSk}.
nodes.statement_short: Solve H_k = Z_k H_{k+1} A^ss_k + S_k by the series operator F with norm L'.

nodes.name: Nonlinear operator Q
nodes.statement: Consider the nonlinear operator $Q:X \to X$ defined as $Q(\{H_k\}) = \{S_k\}$, where $$ S_k = Z_k(- \Delta_k^{us} - \Delta_k^{uu}H_k + H_{k+1}A_k^{su}H_k + H_{k+1}\Delta_k^{ss} + H_{k+1}\Delta_k^{su}H_k). $$ Note that if $\{H_k\} \in X$ is a fixed point of $F \circ Q$, i.e. $\{H_k\} = F \circ Q (\{H_k\})$, then $\{H_k\}$ satisfies~\eqref{eq:StHk}.
nodes.statement_short: Fixed points of F o Q solve the invariance equation.

nodes.name: Contraction
nodes.statement: Let $\varepsilon_2$ satisfy the conditions \eqref{eq:condep1ep2}. Let $U$ be the closed ball in $X$ of radius $\varepsilon_2$ centered at $0$. In the following, we show that $F \circ Q : U \to U$ and $F \circ Q|_{U}$ is a contraction. Consider $H = \{H_k\}, H' = \{H'_k\} \in U$, and assume that $ \|H_k\|, \|H'_k\| \leq \varepsilon_2$, $\|H-H'\| = \delta $. Let us estimate $Q\{H_k\} - Q\{H'_k\} = \{S_k - S'_k\}$. The following holds \begin{multline*} \|S_k - S'_k\| \leq \|Z_k\| \cdot \|-\Delta_k^{uu}(H_k-H_k') + H_{k+1}A_k^{su}H_k -H'_{k+1}A_k^{su}H'_k + \\ (H_{k+1}-H'_{k+1})\Delta_k^{ss} + H_{k+1}\Delta_k^{su}H_k - H'_{k+1}\Delta_k^{su}H'_k\| \leq \\ R(2\varepsilon_1 \delta + (H_{k+1}-H'_{k+1})(A_k^{su}+\Delta_k^{su})H_k + H_{k+1}(A_k^{su}+\Delta_k^{su})(H_k-H'_k) \\ - (H_{k+1}-H'_{k+1})(A_k^{su}+\Delta_k^{su})(H_k-H'_k)) \leq \\ R(2 \varepsilon_1 \delta + 2\delta(R+\varepsilon_1)\varepsilon_2 + (R+\varepsilon_1)\delta^2 ) = R(2\varepsilon_1 + 2(R+\varepsilon_1)\varepsilon_2 + (R+\varepsilon_1)\delta)\delta. \end{multline*} Taking into account \eqref{eq:condep1ep2} and $\delta \leq 2\varepsilon_2$ we conclude that $ \|QH - QH'\| \leq \frac{1}{2L'}\|H-H'\|. $ Since $F$ is linear, inequality \eqref{eq:FL'} implies that \begin{equation} \|F \circ QH - F \circ QH'\| \leq L'\frac{1}{2L'}\|H-H'\| = \frac{1}{2}\|H-H'\|, \end{equation} and hence $F \circ Q$ is contracting on $U$. Note that $\|Q\{H_k = 0\}\| = \|\{-Z_k\Delta_k^{us}\}\| \leq R\varepsilon_1$, hence $ \|F \circ Q\{H_k = 0\}\| \leq L'R\varepsilon_1 $ and according to \eqref{eq:FQcontr} and \eqref{eq:defep1ep2} for any $H \in U$ we have $$ \|F \circ Q H\| \leq \|F\circ QH-F\circ Q\{0\}\|+\|F\circ Q\{0\}\| \leq \varepsilon_2/2 + L'R\varepsilon_1 \leq \varepsilon_2 $$ and hence $F \circ Q(U) \subset U$. By the contraction mapping principle, there exists a unique $H = \{H_k\}$, with $|H_k| \leq \varepsilon_2$ such that $F \circ Q H = H$. Consequently, the subspaces $\tilde{E}_k^s$ defined by \eqref{eq:tildeEDef} satisfy \eqref{eq:ETildaIncl}.
nodes.statement_short: F o Q maps the epsilon_2-ball into itself and contracts; take its fixed point.

nodes.name: Exponential estimates on new stable spaces
nodes.statement: Let us show that for small enough $\varepsilon, \varepsilon_2$ the spaces $\tilde{E}_k^s$ satisfy \begin{equation} |B_{k+n-1} \cdot \ldots \cdot B_k\tilde{v}^s_k| \leq C_1 \lambda_1^n |\tilde{v}^s_k|, \quad \tilde{v}^s_k \in \tilde{E}^s_k, n \geq 0 \end{equation} for some $C_1 = C_1(C, \lambda, \lambda_1, R)$. Indeed, let us choose $N$ such that $2C\lambda^N \leq \lambda_1^N$ and choose $C_1 = \left(\frac{R+1}{\lambda_1}\right)^N$. For small enough $\varepsilon, \varepsilon_2$ we have $$ \|B_{k+N-1} \cdot \ldots \cdot B_k|_{\tilde{E}_k^s}\| \leq 2 \|A_{k+N-1} \cdot \ldots \cdot A_k|_{{E}_k^s}\| \leq 2C\lambda^N \leq \lambda_1^N, \quad k \in \mathbb{Z}. $$ Represent $n > 0$ in the form $n = lN + r$, with $l \geq 0$, $r \in [0, N-1]$. Note that \begin{multline} \|B_{k+n-1} \cdot \ldots \cdot B_k|_{\tilde{E}_k^s}\| \leq \\ \left(\prod_{i = 0}^{l-1}\|B_{k+(i+1)N-1} \cdot \ldots \cdot B_{k+iN}|_{\tilde{E}_{k+iN}^s}\|\right)\|B_{k+lN+r-1} \cdot \ldots \cdot B_{k+lN}|_{\tilde{E}_{k+lN}^s}\| \leq \\ (\lambda_1^N)^l(R+1)^r\leq C_1\lambda_1^n, \end{multline} which implies \eqref{eq:GH3Bs}.
nodes.statement_short: Block estimates of length N give the exponential estimate with C_1, lambda_1.

nodes.name: Block length
nodes.statement: Indeed, let us choose $N$ such that $2C\lambda^N \leq \lambda_1^N$ and choose $C_1 = \left(\frac{R+1}{\lambda_1}\right)^N$. For small enough $\varepsilon, \varepsilon_2$ we have $$ \|B_{k+N-1} \cdot \ldots \cdot B_k|_{\tilde{E}_k^s}\| \leq 2 \|A_{k+N-1} \cdot \ldots \cdot A_k|_{{E}_k^s}\| \leq 2C\lambda^N \leq \lambda_1^N, \quad k \in \mathbb{Z}. $$
nodes.statement_short: Choose N with 2C lambda^N <= lambda_1^N.

nodes.name: Concatenate blocks
nodes.statement: Represent $n > 0$ in the form $n = lN + r$, with $l \geq 0$, $r \in [0, N-1]$. Note that \begin{multline} \|B_{k+n-1} \cdot \ldots \cdot B_k|_{\tilde{E}_k^s}\| \leq \\ \left(\prod_{i = 0}^{l-1}\|B_{k+(i+1)N-1} \cdot \ldots \cdot B_{k+iN}|_{\tilde{E}_{k+iN}^s}\|\right)\|B_{k+lN+r-1} \cdot \ldots \cdot B_{k+lN}|_{\tilde{E}_{k+lN}^s}\| \leq \\ (\lambda_1^N)^l(R+1)^r\leq C_1\lambda_1^n, \end{multline} which implies \eqref{eq:GH3Bs}.
nodes.statement_short: Split n = lN + r and multiply block estimates.

nodes.name: Unstable spaces and projections
nodes.statement: Similarly, for small enough $\varepsilon$ we construct a sequence of operators $H_k^u:E_k^u \to A_{k-1}E_{k-1}^s$ and spaces $\tilde{E}_k^u = \{ v_k^u + H_k^uv_k^u : v_k^u \in E_k^u\}$ such that $ B_k^{-1} \tilde{E}_{k+1}^u \subseteq \tilde{E}_{k}^u $ and \begin{equation} |B_{k-n}^{-1} \cdot \ldots \cdot B_{k-1}^{-1}\tilde{v}^u_k| \leq C_1 \lambda_1^n |\tilde{v}^u_k|, \quad \tilde{v}^u_k \in \tilde{E}^u_k, n \geq 0. \end{equation} For small enough $\varepsilon_2$ the inequalities $\|H_k\|, \|H_k^u\| \leq \varepsilon_2$ imply that the operator \begin{equation}\notag T_k = \begin{bmatrix} Id & H_k^u \\ H_k & Id \end{bmatrix} \end{equation} is invertible, and projections $ P_{\tilde{E}_{k}^{s, u}} = T_k\circ P_{{E}_k^{s, u}} \circ T^{-1}_{k} $ satisfy $\|P_{\tilde{E}_{k}^{s, u}}\| \leq 2C$ and $\tilde{E}_k^s \oplus \tilde{E}_k^u = \mathbb{B}$.
nodes.statement_short: Construct the unstable graphs similarly and bound the new projections.

nodes.name: Conclude (Robust1)
nodes.statement: Hence, the sequence $\mathcal{B}$ satisfies generalized hyperbolicity with spaces $\tilde{E}_k^s, \tilde{E}_k^u$ and constants $C_1, \lambda_1$. Item \textit{(Robust1)} is proved.
nodes.statement_short: B is GH with constants C_1, lambda_1.

nodes.name: Periodic case setup
nodes.statement: To prove item \textit{(Robust2)}, we consider an $m$-periodic sequence of operators $\mathcal{A} = \{A_k\}$ that satisfies periodic generalized hyperbolicity, with the corresponding periodic splitting $\mathbb{B} = E_k^s \oplus E_k^u$. Let $\mathcal{B} = \{B_k\}$ be an $m$-periodic perturbation of $\mathcal{A}$ satisfying \eqref{eq:AkBk}. We show that the subspaces $\tilde{E}_k^s$, $\tilde{E}_k^u$ constructed in the proof of \textit{(Robust1)} are $m$-periodic.
nodes.statement_short: Consider periodic A, B and periodic splitting.

nodes.name: Periodicity of the fixed point
nodes.statement: The sequence of operators $H = \{H_k\} \in X$ satisfying $(F \circ Q)H = H$ can be obtained as a limit of iterates $H^l = (F \circ Q)^l\{H_k = 0\} \in X$: $ H = \lim_{l \to \infty}H^l. $ If sequences $\mathcal{A}$, $\mathcal{B}$ and projections $P_k$, $Q_k$ are $m$-periodic, then the operator $(F \circ Q)$ maps $m$-periodic sequences to $m$-periodic sequences. Hence, for any $l>0$ the iterate $H^l$ is $m$-periodic, and so is its limit $H$. Therefore, the subspaces $\tilde{E}_k^s$ constructed in the proof of item \textit{(Robust1)} are $m$-periodic. Similar considerations show that $\tilde{E}_k^u$ is $m$-periodic as well. Consequently, $\mathcal{B}$ satisfies periodic generalized hyperbolicity. This proves item \textit{(Robust2)}.
nodes.statement_short: Iterates of F o Q stay periodic, so the fixed point and spaces are periodic.

nodes.name: Constants
nodes.statement: Let $M = 2L$. Fix $d_0 > 0$, satisfying the following inequalities \begin{equation} L + 2(RM+R)(RM+R+L)\cdot r\left((RM+R+L)d_0\right) \leq M, \end{equation} \begin{equation} 2 (RM+R+L) \cdot r\left((RM+R+L)d_0\right) < 1. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Fix M = 2L and d_0 satisfying two smallness inequalities.

nodes.name: Symmetric intervals lemma
nodes.statement: We first prove the statement for intervals of the form $[-N,N]$. \begin{lem} For any $d < d_0$ and any $d$-pseudotrajectory $\{y_k\}_{k \in [-N, N]}$ there exists an exact trajectory $\{x_k\}_{k \in [-N, N]}$ such that $ |y_k - x_k| \leq Md $. \end{lem} \begin{proof} We prove the claim by induction on $N$. For $N=0$, the statement is immediate. Consider a $d$-pseudotrajectory $\{y_{k \in [-(N+1), N+1]}\}$ with $d<d_0$. By the induction hypothesis, the $d$-pseudotrajectory $\{y_{k \in [-N, N]}\}$ is $Md$-shadowed by an exact trajectory $\{p_{k \in [-N, N]}\}$ \begin{equation} |y_k - p_k| \leq M d, \quad k \in [-N, N]. \end{equation} Note that $p_{N+1} = f(p_N)$, $p_{-(N+1)} = f^{-1}(p_{-N})$. Due to \eqref{eq:C1-2}, \eqref{eq:pst1}, \eqref{eq:pst2} the following estimates hold \begin{equation} |y_{N+1} - p_{N+1}| \leq (RM+1)d, \quad |y_{-(N+1)} - p_{-(N+1)}| \leq (RM+R)d. \end{equation} Hence, we conclude the following. \begin{statement} For $d< d_0$ a $d$-pseudotrajectory $\{y_{k \in [-(N+1), N+1]}\}$ can be $(RM+R)d$-shadowed. \end{statement} In the following, we show how to construct a better shadowing trajectory. Denote $A_k = Df(p_k)$. Consider the sequence $\{w_k \in \mathbb{B}\}$ defined by $$ y_{k+1} - f(y_k) = - d w_{k+1}, \quad k \in [-(N+1), N], $$ $$ w_{k+1} = 0, \quad k \notin [-(N+1), N]. $$ Note that $|w_k| \leq 1$. By Lemma \ref{lem:SBS} there exists a sequence $\{v_k \in \mathbb{B}\}_{k \in \mathbb{Z}}$, $|v_k| \leq L$ such that equalities \eqref{eq:Inh} hold. Consider the sequence $z_k = y_k + dv_k$. Note that $$ f(z_k) = f(y_k + dv_k) = f(p_k + (y_k-p_k) +dv_k), \quad k \in [-(N+1), N+1]. $$ Inequalities \eqref{eq:C1-1}, \eqref{eq:C1-2}, \eqref{Add4.1}, \eqref{Add4.2} imply that \begin{multline*} |f(z_k) - (f(p_k) + A_k (y_k - p_k + dv_k) )| \leq |y_k - p_k + dv_k|r(|y_k - p_k + dv_k|) \leq \\ (RM+R+L)d \cdot r\left((RM+R+L)d\right). \end{multline*} Then for $k \in [-(N+1), N]$ the following inequalities hold \begin{multline*} |z_{k+1} - f(z_k)| = |y_{k+1} + dv_{k+1} - p_{k+1} - \\ A_k (y_k - p_k + dv_k) - (f(z_k) - (f(p_k) + A_k (y_k - p_k + dv_k) ))| \leq \\ |y_{k+1} - p_{k+1} + dw_{k+1} - A_k (y_k - p_k)| +|f(z_k) - (f(p_k) + A_k (y_k - p_k + dv_k) )| \leq \\ |f(y_k) - f(p_k) - A_k (y_k - p_k)| + (RM+R+L)d \cdot r\left((RM+R+L)d\right) \leq \\ |y_k - p_k|r(|y_k - p_k|) + (RM+R+L)d \cdot r\left((RM+R+L)d\right) \leq \\ (RM+R)d\cdot r((RM+R)d) + (RM+R+L)d \cdot r\left((RM+R+L)d\right) \leq \\ 2 (RM+R+L)d \cdot r\left((RM+R+L)d\right). \end{multline*} Hence $\{z_{k \in [-(N+1), N+1]}\}$ is a $2 (RM+R+L)d \cdot r\left((RM+R+L)d\right)$-pseudotrajectory. Inequality~\eqref{eq:M2''} implies $ 2 (RM+R+L)d \cdot r\left((RM+R+L)d\right) < d_0 $. According to Proposition \ref{stat:dn+1} the pseudotrajectory $\{z_{k \in [-(N+1), N+1]}\}$ can be $2(RM+R)(RM+R+L)d \cdot r\left((RM+R+L)d\right)$-shadowed by an exact trajectory $q_{k \in [-(N+1), N+1]}$. Then by \eqref{eq:M2'} \begin{multline*} |y_k - q_k| \leq |y_k - z_k| + |z_k-q_k| \leq \\ Ld + 2(RM+R)(RM+R+L)d \cdot r\left((RM+R+L)d\right) \leq Md \end{multline*} and the pseudotrajectory $\{y_{k \in [-(N+1), N+1]}\}$ is $Md$-shadowed by $\{q_{k \in [-(N+1), N+1]}\}$, which completes the induction step and proves Lemma \ref{lem:NLipSh}. \end{proof}
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to the lemma on [-N,N], proved by induction.

nodes.name: Base case
nodes.statement: We prove the claim by induction on $N$. For $N=0$, the statement is immediate.
nodes.statement_short: Induction on N; N=0 is immediate.

nodes.name: Inductive hypothesis
nodes.statement: Consider a $d$-pseudotrajectory $\{y_{k \in [-(N+1), N+1]}\}$ with $d<d_0$. By the induction hypothesis, the $d$-pseudotrajectory $\{y_{k \in [-N, N]}\}$ is $Md$-shadowed by an exact trajectory $\{p_{k \in [-N, N]}\}$ \begin{equation} |y_k - p_k| \leq M d, \quad k \in [-N, N]. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Shadow the inner part by the induction hypothesis.

nodes.name: Coarse extension
nodes.statement: Note that $p_{N+1} = f(p_N)$, $p_{-(N+1)} = f^{-1}(p_{-N})$. Due to \eqref{eq:C1-2}, \eqref{eq:pst1}, \eqref{eq:pst2} the following estimates hold \begin{equation} |y_{N+1} - p_{N+1}| \leq (RM+1)d, \quad |y_{-(N+1)} - p_{-(N+1)}| \leq (RM+R)d. \end{equation} Hence, we conclude the following.
nodes.statement_short: Extend p by one step with error (RM+R)d.

nodes.name: Coarse shadowing proposition
nodes.statement: \begin{statement} For $d< d_0$ a $d$-pseudotrajectory $\{y_{k \in [-(N+1), N+1]}\}$ can be $(RM+R)d$-shadowed. \end{statement}
nodes.statement_short: State the coarse shadowing proposition.

nodes.name: Linearized forcing
nodes.statement: In the following, we show how to construct a better shadowing trajectory. Denote $A_k = Df(p_k)$. Consider the sequence $\{w_k \in \mathbb{B}\}$ defined by $$ y_{k+1} - f(y_k) = - d w_{k+1}, \quad k \in [-(N+1), N], $$ $$ w_{k+1} = 0, \quad k \notin [-(N+1), N]. $$ Note that $|w_k| \leq 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce A_k = Df(p_k) and the normalized errors w_k.

nodes.name: Bounded solution
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{lem:SBS} there exists a sequence $\{v_k \in \mathbb{B}\}_{k \in \mathbb{Z}}$, $|v_k| \leq L$ such that equalities \eqref{eq:Inh} hold.
nodes.statement_short: Solve the linearized equation with |v_k| <= L.

nodes.name: Correction
nodes.statement: Consider the sequence $z_k = y_k + dv_k$. Note that $$ f(z_k) = f(y_k + dv_k) = f(p_k + (y_k-p_k) +dv_k), \quad k \in [-(N+1), N+1]. $$ Inequalities \eqref{eq:C1-1}, \eqref{eq:C1-2}, \eqref{Add4.1}, \eqref{Add4.2} imply that \begin{multline*} |f(z_k) - (f(p_k) + A_k (y_k - p_k + dv_k) )| \leq |y_k - p_k + dv_k|r(|y_k - p_k + dv_k|) \leq \\ (RM+R+L)d \cdot r\left((RM+R+L)d\right). \end{multline*}
nodes.statement_short: Correct y by d v and bound the linearization error.

nodes.name: Finer pseudotrajectory
nodes.statement: Then for $k \in [-(N+1), N]$ the following inequalities hold \begin{multline*} |z_{k+1} - f(z_k)| = |y_{k+1} + dv_{k+1} - p_{k+1} - \\ A_k (y_k - p_k + dv_k) - (f(z_k) - (f(p_k) + A_k (y_k - p_k + dv_k) ))| \leq \\ |y_{k+1} - p_{k+1} + dw_{k+1} - A_k (y_k - p_k)| +|f(z_k) - (f(p_k) + A_k (y_k - p_k + dv_k) )| \leq \\ |f(y_k) - f(p_k) - A_k (y_k - p_k)| + (RM+R+L)d \cdot r\left((RM+R+L)d\right) \leq \\ |y_k - p_k|r(|y_k - p_k|) + (RM+R+L)d \cdot r\left((RM+R+L)d\right) \leq \\ (RM+R)d\cdot r((RM+R)d) + (RM+R+L)d \cdot r\left((RM+R+L)d\right) \leq \\ 2 (RM+R+L)d \cdot r\left((RM+R+L)d\right). \end{multline*} Hence $\{z_{k \in [-(N+1), N+1]}\}$ is a $2 (RM+R+L)d \cdot r\left((RM+R+L)d\right)$-pseudotrajectory. Inequality~\eqref{eq:M2''} implies $ 2 (RM+R+L)d \cdot r\left((RM+R+L)d\right) < d_0 $.
nodes.statement_short: z is a much finer pseudotrajectory, below d_0.

nodes.name: Conclude induction
nodes.statement: According to Proposition \ref{stat:dn+1} the pseudotrajectory $\{z_{k \in [-(N+1), N+1]}\}$ can be $2(RM+R)(RM+R+L)d \cdot r\left((RM+R+L)d\right)$-shadowed by an exact trajectory $q_{k \in [-(N+1), N+1]}$. Then by \eqref{eq:M2'} \begin{multline*} |y_k - q_k| \leq |y_k - z_k| + |z_k-q_k| \leq \\ Ld + 2(RM+R)(RM+R+L)d \cdot r\left((RM+R+L)d\right) \leq Md \end{multline*} and the pseudotrajectory $\{y_{k \in [-(N+1), N+1]}\}$ is $Md$-shadowed by $\{q_{k \in [-(N+1), N+1]}\}$, which completes the induction step and proves Lemma \ref{lem:NLipSh}.
nodes.statement_short: Shadow z coarsely and combine to get Md-shadowing of y.

nodes.name: Restrict
nodes.statement: Every finite interval $I\subset\mathbb{Z}$ is contained in $[-N,N]$ for some $N>0$. Restricting the trajectory supplied by Lemma~\ref{lem:NLipSh} to $I$ proves Lemma~\ref{lem:FinLipSh}.
nodes.statement_short: Every finite interval lies in some [-N,N]; restrict.

nodes.name: Choice of d_0
nodes.statement: By \eqref{eq:C1-r2} there exists $d_0 \in (0, d_1)$ such that \begin{equation} M\cdot r(Md_0) < \frac{1}{2}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Choose d_0 with M r(M d_0) < 1/2.

nodes.name: Error-halving proposition
nodes.statement: \begin{statement} For $d_0$ satisfying \eqref{eq:1.1'} and any $d$-pseudotrajectory $\{y_k\}_{k \in \mathbb{Z}}$ with $d<d_0$ there exists $d/2$-pseudotrajectory $\{z_k\}_{k \in \mathbb{Z}}$ such that \begin{equation} |y_k-z_k| < Md. \end{equation} \end{statement} \begin{proof} Consider a $d$-pseudotrajectory $\{y_k\}$ with $d < d_0$. Similarly to the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:FinLipSh} consider the sequence $\{w_{k \in \mathbb{Z}}\}$ defined by \begin{equation} y_{k+1}-f(y_k) = -dw_{k+1}, \quad k \in \mathbb{Z}. \end{equation} Consider $B_k = Df(y_k)$. By the assumptions of Lemma \ref{lem:BS-SH} there exists a sequence $v_k \in \mathbb{B}$ such that $$ v_{k+1} - B_kv_k = w_{k+1}, \quad |v_k| \leq M, \quad k \in \mathbb{Z}. $$ Consider the sequence $\{z_k = y_k + dv_k\}_{k \in \mathbb{Z}}$. By construction, $\{z_k\}$ satisfies \eqref{eq:d2}. We now show that $\{z_k\}$ is a $d/2$-pseudotrajectory. By the construction of the sequence $\{v_k\}$ we have \begin{equation} y_{k+1} + dv_{k+1} - (f(y_k) + B_kdv_k) = 0. \end{equation} Due to \eqref{eq:C1-1}, \eqref{eq:1.1'} and \eqref{eq:zkBk} the following inequalities hold \begin{multline*} |z_{k+1} - f(z_k)| = |y_{k+1} + dv_{k+1} - (f(y_k)+B_kdv_k) - (f(y_k+dv_k) - f(y_k) -B_kdv_k)| = \\ |f(y_k+dv_k) - f(y_k) -B_kdv_k| \leq d|v_k|r(d|v_k|) \leq Md \cdot r(Md) \leq \frac{d}{2}. \end{multline*} Proposition \ref{stat:d2} is proved. \end{proof}
nodes.statement_short: State and prove the error-halving proposition.

nodes.name: Normalized errors
nodes.statement: Consider a $d$-pseudotrajectory $\{y_k\}$ with $d < d_0$. Similarly to the proof of Lemma~\ref{lem:FinLipSh} consider the sequence $\{w_{k \in \mathbb{Z}}\}$ defined by \begin{equation} y_{k+1}-f(y_k) = -dw_{k+1}, \quad k \in \mathbb{Z}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Define the normalized one-step errors w_k.

nodes.name: Bounded solution
nodes.statement: Consider $B_k = Df(y_k)$. By the assumptions of Lemma \ref{lem:BS-SH} there exists a sequence $v_k \in \mathbb{B}$ such that $$ v_{k+1} - B_kv_k = w_{k+1}, \quad |v_k| \leq M, \quad k \in \mathbb{Z}. $$
nodes.statement_short: Use the bounded solution property for B_k = Df(y_k).

nodes.name: Correction
nodes.statement: Consider the sequence $\{z_k = y_k + dv_k\}_{k \in \mathbb{Z}}$. By construction, $\{z_k\}$ satisfies \eqref{eq:d2}.
nodes.statement_short: Set z = y + d v, which is Md-close to y.

nodes.name: z is a d/2-pseudotrajectory
nodes.statement: We now show that $\{z_k\}$ is a $d/2$-pseudotrajectory. By the construction of the sequence $\{v_k\}$ we have \begin{equation} y_{k+1} + dv_{k+1} - (f(y_k) + B_kdv_k) = 0. \end{equation} Due to \eqref{eq:C1-1}, \eqref{eq:1.1'} and \eqref{eq:zkBk} the following inequalities hold \begin{multline*} |z_{k+1} - f(z_k)| = |y_{k+1} + dv_{k+1} - (f(y_k)+B_kdv_k) - (f(y_k+dv_k) - f(y_k) -B_kdv_k)| = \\ |f(y_k+dv_k) - f(y_k) -B_kdv_k| \leq d|v_k|r(d|v_k|) \leq Md \cdot r(Md) \leq \frac{d}{2}. \end{multline*} Proposition \ref{stat:d2} is proved.
nodes.statement_short: The one-step error of z is the nonlinear remainder, at most d/2.

nodes.name: Linear identity
nodes.statement: By the construction of the sequence $\{v_k\}$ we have \begin{equation} y_{k+1} + dv_{k+1} - (f(y_k) + B_kdv_k) = 0. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The linearized equation holds exactly.

nodes.name: Remainder bound
nodes.statement: Due to \eqref{eq:C1-1}, \eqref{eq:1.1'} and \eqref{eq:zkBk} the following inequalities hold \begin{multline*} |z_{k+1} - f(z_k)| = |y_{k+1} + dv_{k+1} - (f(y_k)+B_kdv_k) - (f(y_k+dv_k) - f(y_k) -B_kdv_k)| = \\ |f(y_k+dv_k) - f(y_k) -B_kdv_k| \leq d|v_k|r(d|v_k|) \leq Md \cdot r(Md) \leq \frac{d}{2}. \end{multline*} Proposition \ref{stat:d2} is proved.
nodes.statement_short: Bound the remainder by M d r(Md) <= d/2.

nodes.name: Iterative scheme
nodes.statement: Continue the proof of Lemma \ref{lem:BS-SH}. For a given $d$-pseudotrajectory $\{y_k\}_{k \in \mathbb{Z}}$ with $d< d_0$ consider the sequence of $\delta_l$-pseudotrajectories $\{y_k^l\}_{k \in \mathbb{Z}}$ defined inductively.
nodes.statement_short: Build a sequence of pseudotrajectories inductively.

nodes.name: Iterate halving
nodes.statement: Define $\delta_0 = d$, $\{y_k^0 = y_k\}_{k \in \mathbb{Z}}$. By a given $\delta_l$-pseudotrajectory $\{y_k^l\}_{k \in \mathbb{Z}}$ with $\delta_l < d_0$ according to Proposition \ref{stat:d2} choose $\delta_{l+1} = \delta_l/2$-pseudotrajectory $\{y_k^{l+1}\}$ such that $ |y_k^{l+1} - y_k^l| \leq M \delta_l. $ By construction we have $\delta_l = \frac{d}{2^l}$ and \begin{equation} |y_{k+1}^l - f(y_k^l)| \leq \frac{d}{2^l}, \quad |y_k^{l+1} - y_k^l| \leq M\frac{d}{2^l}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Apply the halving step repeatedly: errors d/2^l, displacements M d/2^l.

nodes.name: Cauchy limit
nodes.statement: Hence, for any fixed $k \in \mathbb{Z}$, the sequence $\{y_k^l\}$ is a Cauchy sequence with respect to $l$ and there exists a limit $ x_k = \lim_{l \to \infty} y_k^l. $ Note that \begin{equation} |y_k - x_k| = |y_k^0 - x_k| \leq \sum_{l\geq 0} |y_k^l-y_k^{l+1}| \leq \sum_{l\geq 0}M\frac{d}{2^l} = 2Md. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Cauchy sequences converge, with total displacement 2Md.

nodes.name: Exact trajectory
nodes.statement: The continuity of $f$ and condition \eqref{eq:3.1-3.2} imply that $x_{k+1} = f(x_k)$. Therefore, $\{x_k\}$ is an exact trajectory of $f$ that $2Md$-shadows $\{y_k\}$. Lemma \ref{lem:BS-SH} is proved.
nodes.statement_short: The limit is an exact trajectory shadowing y.

nodes.name: Collect constants
nodes.statement: Now we show that the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{thm:main-results}\,(\ref{item:main-LipSh}) imply the hypotheses of Lemma~\ref{lem:BS-SH}. By Lemma \ref{lem:FinLipSh}, the map $f$ satisfies the finite Lipschitz shadowing property. Let $L > 0$ be the constant from Lemma \ref{lem:SBS}, let $\varepsilon > 0$ be the constant from Lemma \ref{lem:SBS-robust}, and let $M, d_0$ be the constants from the finite Lipschitz shadowing property.
nodes.statement_short: Collect FinLipSh, L from Lemma SBS and epsilon from Lemma SBS-robust.

nodes.name: Choose d_1
nodes.statement: By condition \eqref{eq:C1-r1}, choose $\delta > 0$ such that if $|x - y|< \delta$ we have $\|Df(x)-Df(y)\| < \varepsilon$. Set $d_1 := \min(d_0, \delta/M)$. Fix $d<d_1$ and a $d$-pseudotrajectory $\{y_k\}_{k \in \mathbb{Z}}$. Define the sequence of operators $\mathcal{B} = \{B_k = Df(y_k)\}_{k \in \mathbb{Z}}$. We claim that the sequence $\mathcal{B}$ satisfies the bounded solution property with constant $4L$.
nodes.statement_short: Choose delta and d_1 and state the claim of constant 4L.

nodes.name: Verify bounded solutions
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{lem:FinLipSh}, for any finite interval $I \subset \mathbb{Z}$ the sequence $\{y_k\}_{k \in I}$ can be $Md$-shadowed by an exact trajectory $\{x_k\}_{k \in I}$. Set $\{A_k = Df(x_k)\}_{k \in I}$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:SBS} it satisfies the strong bounded solution property with constant $L$. Moreover, since $Md < \delta$ we have $\|B_k - A_k\| \leq \varepsilon$, $k \in I$. By Lemma \ref{lem:SBS-robust}, the sequence $\{B_k\}_{k \in I}$ satisfies the bounded solution property with constant~$2L$. Lemma~\ref{lem:Bk-Inf} implies that $\{B_k\}_{k \in \mathbb{Z}}$ satisfies the bounded solution property with constant~$4L$. Therefore, the hypotheses of Lemma \ref{lem:BS-SH} hold, which completes the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:main-results}\,(\ref{item:main-LipSh}).
nodes.statement_short: Finite shadowing, strong bounded solutions, robustness and the finite-to-infinite lemma give constant 4L.

nodes.name: Nonperiodic shadowing
nodes.statement: Let $\{y_k\}$ be an $m$-periodic $d$-pseudotrajectory. By Theorem~\ref{thm:main-results}\,(\ref{item:main-LipSh}), there exists $M > 0$ such that $\{y_k\}$ is $Md$-shadowed by an exact trajectory (not necessarily periodic) $\{x_k\}$: $$ \mathrm{dist}(y_k, x_k) \leq Md, \quad k \in \mathbb{Z}. $$
nodes.statement_short: Shadow the periodic pseudotrajectory by an exact, possibly nonperiodic, trajectory.

nodes.name: GH of differentials
nodes.statement: Define the sequences of the linear maps $\mathcal{B} = \{B_k := Df(y_k)\}$ and $\mathcal{A} = \{A_k := Df(x_k)\}$. Since $f$ satisfies generalized hyperbolicity, the sequence $\mathcal{A}$ satisfies generalized hyperbolicity as well. By item (Robust1) of Lemma~\ref{lem:CL-robust-Ak}, for any $\lambda_1 \in (\lambda, 1)$ there exists $C_1 = C_1(C, \lambda, \lambda_1, R) > 0$ such that, for sufficiently small $d$, the sequence $\mathcal{B}$ also satisfies generalized hyperbolicity with constants $C_1$, $\lambda_1$.
nodes.statement_short: By (Robust1) the differentials along y are GH.

nodes.name: Periodic bounded solution
nodes.statement: Consider the $m$-periodic sequence $\{w_k \in \mathbb{B}\}$ defined by~\eqref{eq:defw}. By Lemma~\ref{lem:SBS-periodic}, there exist $L = L(C_1, \lambda_1) > 0$ and an $m$-periodic sequence $\{v_k \in \mathbb{B}\}$ such that $$ v_{k+1} = B_k v_k + w_{k+1}, \quad \text{and} \quad \|v_k\| \leq L. $$
nodes.statement_short: Lemma SBS-periodic gives a periodic bounded solution.

nodes.name: Periodic halving
nodes.statement: Using an argument as in Proposition~\ref{stat:d2}, and reducing $d$ if necessary, there exists a constant $M_1 > 0$ such that the sequence $y_k^1 := y_k + d v_k$, $k \in \mathbb{Z}$, is an $m$ -periodic $d/2$ -pseudotrajectory and, furthermore, satisfies $\|y_k - y_k^1\| \leq M_1 d$.
nodes.statement_short: The correction gives a periodic d/2-pseudotrajectory.

nodes.name: Iterate and pass to limit
nodes.statement: By iterating this construction, as in the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:main-results}\,(\ref{item:main-LipSh}), we obtain a sequence of $m$-periodic pseudotrajectories $\{y_k^l\}_{l \geq 1}$ satisfying the following estimates (compare with~\eqref{eq:3.1-3.2}): $$ \|y_{k+1}^l - f(y_k^l)\| \leq \frac{d}{2^l}, \quad \|y_k^{l+1} - y_k^l\| \leq M_1 \frac{d}{2^l}. $$ Taking the pointwise limit $z_k := \lim_{l \to \infty} y_k^l$, we obtain an $m$-periodic exact trajectory, similarly to~\eqref{eq:42.5}, satisfying $ \|y_k - z_k\| \leq 2M_1 d. $ This completes the proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:main-results}\,(\ref{item:main-LipPerSh}).
nodes.statement_short: Iterate and take the limit: a periodic exact trajectory within 2M_1 d.

nodes.name: Fix chain-recurrent point
nodes.statement: Let $M, d_0 > 0$ be the constants from the Lipschitz periodic shadowing property in Theorem~\ref{thm:main-results}\,(\ref{item:main-LipPerSh}). Fix $x \in CR(f)$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix constants of LipPerSh and x in CR(f).

nodes.name: Periodic pseudotrajectory
nodes.statement: For any $d \in (0, d_0)$ consider a finite pseudotrajectory $y_{k \in [0, N]}$ such that $y_0 = y_N = x$. This segment can be continued to an $N$-periodic pseudotrajectory $$ y_{k+iN} = y_k, \quad k \in [0, N-1], i \in \mathbb{Z}. $$
nodes.statement_short: Close the chain into a periodic pseudotrajectory.

nodes.name: Periodic shadowing
nodes.statement: By Theorem~\ref{thm:main-results}\,(\ref{item:main-LipPerSh}) there exists an $N$-periodic exact trajectory $x_k^{(d)}$ that $Md$-shadows $\{y_k\}$; in particular $ |x - x_0^{(d)}| = |y_0 - x_0^{(d)}| \leq Md $. Since $x_0^{(d)} \in Per(f)$ it follows that $\overline{Per(f)} = CR(f)$.
nodes.statement_short: A periodic orbit Md-close to x; so x is in the closure of Per(f).

nodes.name: Strategy
nodes.statement: The proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:main-results}\,(\ref{item:main-robust}) combines Theorem~\ref{thm:main-results}\,(\ref{item:main-LipSh})--(\ref{item:main-LipPerSh}) with the robustness of generalized hyperbolicity for sequences of operators (Lemma~\ref{lem:CL-robust-Ak}).
nodes.statement_short: Combine shadowing with robustness for sequences.

nodes.name: Constants
nodes.statement: Indeed, consider a diffeomorphism $f:\mathbb{B} \to \mathbb{B}$ satisfying generalized hyperbolicity with constants $C, \lambda$. Fix $\lambda_1 \in (\lambda, 1)$. For any trajectory $\{x_k\}$, the sequence of linear operators $\{Df(x_k)\}$ satisfies generalized hyperbolicity. Take $M, d_0 > 0$ as in Theorem~\ref{thm:main-results}\, (\ref{item:main-LipSh})--(\ref{item:main-LipPerSh}) and $\varepsilon > 0, C_1 > C$ provided by Lemma~\ref{lem:CL-robust-Ak}. Choose $\delta \in (0, \min(d_0, \varepsilon/2))$ such that \begin{equation} \|Df(x)-Df(y)\| \leq \varepsilon/2, \quad |x-y| < M\delta. \end{equation} Let $g\in\mathfrak{D}(\mathbb{B})$ satisfy \begin{equation} \|f-g\|_{C^1}<\delta. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Fix lambda_1, M, d_0, epsilon, C_1 and delta; take g delta-close to f.

nodes.name: Choose base points
nodes.statement: Consider the set $\mathcal{O}$ of all trajectories of the diffeomorphism $g$. For any trajectory $\omega \in \mathcal{O}$ choose a point $y_{\omega} \in \omega$.
nodes.statement_short: Choose a base point on each g-orbit.

nodes.name: g-orbits are pseudo-orbits of f
nodes.statement: We now construct spaces $E_y^{s, u}$ for all points $y \in \omega$. Consider an exact trajectory $y_{k\in \mathbb{Z}}$ of diffeomorphism $g$ with $y_0 = y_{\omega}$. Note that $|y_{k+1} - f(y_k)| = |g(y_k) - f(y_k)| \leq \delta$, $k \in \mathbb{Z}$, hence $y_k$ is a $\delta$-pseudotrajectory of the diffeomorphism $f$. Denote $B_k = Dg(y_k)$. Consider two cases.
nodes.statement_short: Each g-orbit is a delta-pseudotrajectory of f; set B_k = Dg(y_k).

nodes.name: Nonperiodic orbit
nodes.statement: \textbf{Case 1.} If the sequence $\{y_{k}\}$ is not periodic, then the points $\{y_k\}$ are pairwise distinct. By Theorem~\ref{thm:main-results}\,(\ref{item:main-LipSh}) there exists an exact trajectory $\{x_k\}$ of diffeomorphism $f$ that $M\delta$-shadows~$\{y_k\}$: \begin{equation} |y_k-x_k| \leq M\delta, \quad x_{k+1} = f(x_k), \quad k \in \mathbb{Z}. \end{equation} Denote $A_k = Df(x_k)$. According to \eqref{eq:delta1}, \eqref{eq:delta2} the following holds \begin{equation} \|A_k - B_k\| \leq \|A_k - Df(y_k)\| + \|Df(y_k) - B_k\| \leq \varepsilon/2 + \delta < \varepsilon. \end{equation} By item (Robust1) in Lemma \ref{lem:CL-robust-Ak}, the sequence $\{B_k\}$ satisfies generalized hyperbolicity with constants $C_1, \lambda_1$.
nodes.statement_short: Shadow by an f-orbit and apply (Robust1).

nodes.name: Periodic orbit
nodes.statement: \textbf{Case 2.} Suppose that the sequence $\{y_{k}\}$ is $m$-periodic. Then the sequence $\{B_k\}$ is $m$-periodic as well. By Theorem~\ref{thm:main-results}\,(\ref{item:main-LipPerSh}), there exists an $m$-periodic exact trajectory $\{x_k\}$ satisfying \eqref{eq:robustykxk}. The sequence $\{A_k = Df(x_k)\}$ is $m$-periodic and satisfies \eqref{eq:robustAkBk}. By item (Robust2) in Lemma \ref{lem:CL-robust-Ak}, the sequence $\{B_k\}$ satisfies $m$-periodic generalized hyperbolicity with constants $C_1, \lambda_1$.
nodes.statement_short: Shadow by a periodic f-orbit and apply (Robust2).

nodes.name: Assemble splitting
nodes.statement: In both cases denote the spaces corresponding to generalized hyperbolicity for $\{B_k\}$ by $\tilde{E}_k^s$, $\tilde{E}_k^u$. Define (slightly abusing notation) for point~$y_k$ the spaces \begin{equation} \tilde{E}_{y_k}^{s, u} := \tilde{E}_k^{s, u}. \end{equation} If $\omega$ is an $m$-periodic trajectory, then $\tilde{E}_k^{s, u} = \tilde{E}_{k+m}^{s, u}$, and hence $\tilde{E}_{y_k}^{s, u}$ is well-defined. Moreover, Definition \ref{def:CLf} does not impose any condition on the dependence of $E_y^{s, u}$ and the corresponding projections on the point $y$. Hence the splitting defined by \eqref{eq:Eg} satisfies the conditions of generalized hyperbolicity in Definition \ref{def:CLf}.
nodes.statement_short: Define the splitting pointwise along orbits; it satisfies GH for g.

nodes.name: Series definition
nodes.statement: Consider the operator $S_{\alpha, A}:X \to Y$ as in Lemma \ref{lem:SBS}. Given $w \in X$, define $v = S_{\alpha, A}w$ by \begin{equation} v(x) = \sum_{i \leq 0} A^{-i}_{\alpha}(\alpha^i(x)) P_{\alpha^i(x)}w(\alpha^i(x)) -\sum_{i>0}A^{-i}_{\alpha}(\alpha^i(x))Q_{\alpha^i(x)}w(\alpha^i(x)). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Define S w by Perron-type sums along alpha-orbits.

nodes.name: Convergence and continuity
nodes.statement: As in Lemma \ref{lem:SBS}, the series \eqref{eq:Svdef} converges for every $x$ and defines a function $v$ that satisfies \eqref{eq:Twv}. Moreover, $|v(x)| \leq L\|w\|$, where $L = C^2\frac{1+\lambda}{1-\lambda}$. Define $v_N(x)$ analogously by truncating the sum in \eqref{eq:Svdef} to $|i| \leq N$. Then $v_N \to v$ uniformly and since each $v_N$ is uniformly continuous, $v$ is also uniformly continuous.
nodes.statement_short: The series converges, is bounded by L||w|| and is uniformly continuous.

nodes.name: Values in Y; surjectivity
nodes.statement: The first sum in \eqref{eq:Svdef} takes values in $E_x^s$, and the second sum takes values in $F_x$. Hence, $v(x) \in E_x^s \oplus F_x$ and $v \in Y$. Therefore, $S_{\alpha, A}$ is well-defined and satisfies $ T_{\alpha, A}S_{\alpha, A} = Id$, $\|S_{\alpha, A}\| \leq L, $ so $T_{\alpha, A}: Y \to X$ is surjective.
nodes.statement_short: S maps into Y and is a right inverse, so T: Y -> X is onto.

nodes.name: Trivial kernel
nodes.statement:
We now show that its kernel is trivial. Assume that for some $v \in Y$, $v 
e 0$,  egin{equation} T_{\alpha, A}v = 0. \end{equation} Consider $x \in \mathbb{B}$ such that $v(x) 
e 0$. Relation \eqref{eq:KerT} implies that $$ v(\alpha^n(x)) = A^n_{\alpha}(x)v(x), \quad n \in \mathbb{Z}. $$ Denote $v_n = v(\alpha^n(x)) \in E^s_{\alpha^n(x)} \oplus F_{\alpha^n(x)}$. Define $v_n = v_n^s + v_n^u$, where $v_n^s \in E^s_{\alpha^n(x)}$, $v_n^u \in F_{\alpha^n(x)}$. Note that $$ A(\alpha^n(x)) v_n^s \in E_{\alpha^{n+1}(x)}^s, \quad A(\alpha^n(x)) v_n^u \in E_{\alpha^{n+1}(x)}^u. $$ Hence, $$ v_{n+1}^s = A(\alpha^n(x)) v_n^s, \quad v_{n+1}^u = A(\alpha^n(x)) v_n^u, \quad n \in \mathbb{Z}. $$ By induction, we conclude $$ v_{n+k}^s = A^k_{\alpha}(\alpha^n(x)) v_n^s, \quad v_{n+k}^u = A^k_{\alpha}(\alpha^n(x)) v_n^u, \quad n, k \in \mathbb{Z}. $$ Conditions (C-GH1), (C-GH3) imply that $$ |v_{-n}| \geq  rac{1}{C^2}\lambda^{-n} |v_{0}^s|, \quad |v_{n}| \geq  rac{1}{C^2}\lambda^{-n} |v_{0}^u|, \quad n > 0. $$ Note that  egin{itemize} \item if $v_{0}^s 
e 0$ then the values $|v_{-n}|$, $n \geq 0$ are unbounded, \item if $v_{0}^u 
e 0$ then the values $|v_{n}|$, $n \geq 0$ are unbounded. \end{itemize} Since $v(x) 
e 0$, at least one of $v_0^s$, $v_0^u$ is nonzero, so the sequence $\{v(\alpha^n(x))\}_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}$ is unbounded; this is impossible, since $v \in Y \subset X$ is bounded. This shows that the kernel of $T_{\alpha, A}: Y 	o X$ is trivial, so $T_{\alpha, A}$ is injective.
nodes.statement_short: A nonzero kernel element would be unbounded along an orbit.

nodes.name: Assume nonzero kernel element
nodes.statement: Assume that for some $v \in Y$, $v \ne 0$, \begin{equation} T_{\alpha, A}v = 0. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Assume T v = 0 with v nonzero.

nodes.name: Orbit relation
nodes.statement: Consider $x \in \mathbb{B}$ such that $v(x) \ne 0$. Relation \eqref{eq:KerT} implies that $$ v(\alpha^n(x)) = A^n_{\alpha}(x)v(x), \quad n \in \mathbb{Z}. $$
nodes.statement_short: Along the orbit of x, v is transported by the cocycle.

nodes.name: Split components
nodes.statement: Denote $v_n = v(\alpha^n(x)) \in E^s_{\alpha^n(x)} \oplus F_{\alpha^n(x)}$. Define $v_n = v_n^s + v_n^u$, where $v_n^s \in E^s_{\alpha^n(x)}$, $v_n^u \in F_{\alpha^n(x)}$. Note that $$ A(\alpha^n(x)) v_n^s \in E_{\alpha^{n+1}(x)}^s, \quad A(\alpha^n(x)) v_n^u \in E_{\alpha^{n+1}(x)}^u. $$ Hence, $$ v_{n+1}^s = A(\alpha^n(x)) v_n^s, \quad v_{n+1}^u = A(\alpha^n(x)) v_n^u, \quad n \in \mathbb{Z}. $$ By induction, we conclude $$ v_{n+k}^s = A^k_{\alpha}(\alpha^n(x)) v_n^s, \quad v_{n+k}^u = A^k_{\alpha}(\alpha^n(x)) v_n^u, \quad n, k \in \mathbb{Z}. $$
nodes.statement_short: Both components E^s and F are transported separately.

nodes.name: Growth estimates
nodes.statement: Conditions (C-GH1), (C-GH3) imply that $$ |v_{-n}| \geq \frac{1}{C^2}\lambda^{-n} |v_{0}^s|, \quad |v_{n}| \geq \frac{1}{C^2}\lambda^{-n} |v_{0}^u|, \quad n > 0. $$ Note that \begin{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Exponential growth backwards of the stable part, forwards of the F part.

nodes.name: Stable part unbounded
nodes.statement: if $v_{0}^s \ne 0$ then the values $|v_{-n}|$, $n \geq 0$ are unbounded,
nodes.statement_short: A nonzero stable part makes v unbounded backwards.

nodes.name: Unstable part unbounded
nodes.statement: if $v_{0}^u \ne 0$ then the values $|v_{n}|$, $n \geq 0$ are unbounded. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: A nonzero F part makes v unbounded forwards.

nodes.name: Contradiction
nodes.statement: Since $v(x) \ne 0$, at least one of $v_0^s$, $v_0^u$ is nonzero, so the sequence $\{v(\alpha^n(x))\}_{n \in \mathbb{Z}}$ is unbounded; this is impossible, since $v \in Y \subset X$ is bounded. This shows that the kernel of $T_{\alpha, A}: Y \to X$ is trivial, so $T_{\alpha, A}$ is injective.
nodes.statement_short: This contradicts boundedness of v, so T is injective.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Hence, $T_{\alpha, A}$ is invertible and $S_{\alpha, A}$ is its inverse.
nodes.statement_short: T restricted to Y is invertible with inverse S.

nodes.name: Strategy
nodes.statement: The proof uses ideas similar to those in Lemma \ref{lem:CL-robust-Ak}. We highlight the main differences.
nodes.statement_short: Follow the sequence robustness proof; highlight differences.

nodes.name: Block operators
nodes.statement: First, we make a construction of $\tilde{E}^s_x$. Fix $\varepsilon >0$, $\lambda_1 \in (\lambda, 1)$. Denote $F_x = A(x)^{-1}E^u_{\alpha(x)}$ \begin{minipage}{0.49\textwidth} \begin{align*} A_x^{ss}: E_x^s \to \mathbb{B}, & \quad A_x^{ss} = P_{\alpha(x)}A(x),\\ A_x^{su}: E_x^u \to \mathbb{B}, & \quad A_x^{su} = P_{\alpha(x)}A(x),\\ A_x^{us}: E_x^s \to \mathbb{B}, & \quad A_x^{us} = Q_{\alpha(x)}A(x),\\ A_x^{uu}: E_x^u \to \mathbb{B}, & \quad A_x^{uu} = Q_{\alpha(x)}A(x), \end{align*} \end{minipage} \hfill \begin{minipage}{0.49\textwidth} \begin{align*} B_x^{ss}: E_x^s \to \mathbb{B}, & \quad B_x^{ss} = P_{\beta(x)}A(x),\\ B_x^{su}: E_x^u \to \mathbb{B}, & \quad B_x^{su} = P_{\beta(x)}A(x),\\ B_x^{us}: E_x^s \to \mathbb{B}, & \quad B_x^{us} = Q_{\beta(x)}A(x),\\ B_x^{uu}: E_x^u \to \mathbb{B}, & \quad B_x^{uu} = Q_{\beta(x)}A(x), \end{align*} \end{minipage} \smallskip According to (C-GH2) \begin{equation} A^{us}_x = 0. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Define the block operators of A for alpha and beta; A^us = 0.

nodes.name: Closeness of blocks
nodes.statement: Since $P_x, Q_x$ depend uniformly continuously on $x$, for any $\varepsilon_1 \in (0, 1)$ there exists $\delta > 0$ such that, if $\beta$ satisfies \eqref{eq:al-be-ep}, then \begin{equation} \|A_x^{ss} - B_x^{ss}\|, \|A_x^{us} - B_x^{us}\|,\|A_x^{su} - B_x^{su}\|,\|A_x^{uu} - B_x^{uu}\| < \varepsilon_1, \quad x \in \mathbb{B}. \end{equation} Define $J_x: E^u_{\alpha(x)} \to E^u_{\beta(x)}$ as $J_x := Q_{\beta(x)}|_{E^u_{\alpha(x)}}$, then $J_x$ is an isomorphism, and \begin{equation}\notag |J_x v_1 - v_1| \leq \varepsilon_1 |v_1|, \; |J^{-1}_x v_2 - v_2| \leq \varepsilon_1 |v_2|, \quad x \in \mathbb{B}, v_1 \in E^u_{\alpha(x)}, v_2 \in E^u_{\beta(x)}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Uniform continuity makes the alpha- and beta-blocks epsilon_1-close; define J_x.

nodes.name: Claims (B1)
nodes.statement: In the following we show that for any $\lambda_2 \in (\lambda, \lambda_1)$ there exists $C_2 > 0$ and small enough~$\varepsilon_1$ such that $B^{ss}$ and $B^{uu}$ satisfy \begin{itemize} \item[\textbf{(B1)}] $ \|B^{ss}_{\beta^{n-1}(x)} \dots B^{ss}_{\beta(x)}B^{ss}_x\| \leq C_2\lambda_2^n, \quad n \geq 0, x \in \mathbb{B}, $
nodes.statement_short: State the block estimates (B1).

nodes.name: Claim (B2)
nodes.statement: [\textbf{(B2)}] $B^{uu}_{x}$ has the right inverse $Z_x: E_{\beta(x)}^u \to F_x$ such that \begin{equation} B^{uu}_{x} Z_x = Id|_{E_{\beta(x)}^u}, \|Z_x\| \leq (1+\varepsilon_1)R, \end{equation} \begin{equation} \|Z_{\beta^{-n}(x)} \dots Z_{\beta^{-2}(x)}Z_{\beta^{-1}(x)}\| \leq C_2\lambda_2^n, \quad n \geq 0, x \in \mathbb{B}. \end{equation} \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: State the right-inverse estimates (B2).

nodes.name: Proof of (B1)
nodes.statement: The proof of \textbf{(B1)} is similar to the argument in \eqref{eq:GH3Bs}. Fix $\lambda_2$ and choose $N$ so that $2C\lambda^N \leq \lambda_2^N$. Set $C_2=(R(C+2)/\lambda_2)^N$. Note that for any $\delta_1 > 0$ there exists $\delta > 0$ such that, whenever $\beta$ satisfies \eqref{eq:al-be-ep}, it holds $ \mathrm{dist}(\beta^n(x), \alpha^n(x)) \leq \delta_1 $ , $(n \in [1, N])$. For small enough~$\delta_1$ we have $$ \|B^{ss}_{\beta^{N-1}(x)} \dots B^{ss}_{\beta(x)}B^{ss}_x\| \leq 2\|A^{ss}_{\alpha^{N-1}(x)} \dots A^{ss}_{\alpha(x)}A^{ss}_x\|. $$ Similarly to \eqref{eq:B-proof} we conclude \textbf{(B1)}.
nodes.statement_short: Compare N-step products along alpha and beta orbits and concatenate blocks.

nodes.name: Proof of (B2)
nodes.statement: The proof of \textbf{(B2)} is similar to the argument in \textbf{(B1)} and \eqref{eq:GH3Bs-inv}. Choosing $N$ as in \textbf{(B1)}, reducing additionally $\delta_1$ we may assume that $ \mathrm{dist}(\beta^{-n}(x), \alpha^{-n}(x)) \leq \delta_1 $, $(n \in [1, N])$. Define $Z_x = A(x)^{-1}J_x^{-1}$, which satisfies \eqref{eq:Zx-cond}. As in \textbf{(B1)}, we conclude that $$ \|Z_{\beta^{-N}(x)} \dots Z_{\beta^{-2}(x)}Z_{\beta^{-1}(x)}\| \leq 2 \|A^{-1}_{\alpha^{-N}(x)} \dots A^{-1}_{\alpha^{-2}(x)}A^{-1}_{\alpha^{-1}(x)}|_{E_x^u}\| \leq 2C\lambda^N \leq \lambda_2^N. $$ For arbitrary $n\geq0$, write $n=lN+r$, where $l\geq0$ and $0\leq r<N$. Splitting the product into blocks of length $N$ and using $\|Z_x\|\leq(1+\varepsilon_1)R$, we obtain \eqref{eq:Zx-exp}. Item \textbf{(B2)} is proved.
nodes.statement_short: Define Z_x = A^{-1}J^{-1} and concatenate N-blocks.

nodes.name: Invariance equation for H^s
nodes.statement: In the following, we construct a map $H_x^s:E_x^s \to F_x$ with the following property: for any $v^s \in E^s_x$ there exists $w^s \in E_{\beta(x)}^s$ such that \begin{equation} A(x)(v^s+ H^s_xv^s) = w^s+ H^s_{\beta(x)}(w^s) \end{equation} For an arbitrary map $H_x^s$ we can represent $A(x)(v^s+ H^s_x(v^s)) = w^s + w^u$, where \begin{equation*} w^s = B^{ss}_x v^s + B^{su}_x H^s_xv^s \in E^s_{\beta(x)}, \quad w^u = B^{us}_x v^s + B^{uu}_x H^s_xv^s \in E^u_{\beta(x)}. \end{equation*} Condition \eqref{eq:Hsx-cond1} is equivalent to $w^u = H^s_{\beta(x)}w^s$, i.e., \begin{equation} B^{uu}_x H^s_x = H_{\beta(x)}^s(B^{ss}_x + B^{su}_xH^s_x) - B^{us}_x. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Invariance of the graph of H^s reduces to an operator equation.

nodes.name: Fixed-point form
nodes.statement: To satisfy \eqref{eq:H-via-B} it is sufficient to verify the following (compare with \eqref{eq:StHk}) \begin{equation} H_x^s = Z_x H^s_{\beta(x)} B_x^{ss} + (Z_x H^s_{\beta(x)}B^{su}_xH^s_x - Z_xB^{us}_x). \end{equation} As in Section \ref{sec:robust-Ak}, we consider the following auxiliary problem. Given a family of bounded linear operators $S_x:E^s_x \to F_x$ that depends uniformly continuously on $x$, we seek a family of bounded linear operators $H_x: E^s_x \to F_x$ that depends uniformly continuously on $x$, which satisfies $ H_x = Z_xH_{\beta(x)}B_x^{ss} + S_x $ (compare to \eqref{eq:HkSk}).
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite as H = Z H B^ss + S with an auxiliary linear problem.

nodes.name: Series operator F
nodes.statement: Denote by $U$ the Banach space of uniformly bounded linear operators $S_x : E^s_x \to F_x$ that depend uniformly continuously on $x$. Define an operator $F: U \to U$ by $F(S_x) = H_x$, where \begin{equation}\notag H_x = S_x + \sum_{l = 1}^{+\infty}Z_x\cdot \ldots \cdot Z_{\beta^{l-1}(x)}S_{\beta^{l}(x)}B_{\beta^{l-1}(x)}^{ss} \cdot \ldots \cdot B_x^{ss}. \end{equation} Similarly to \eqref{eq:FL'} the following holds \begin{equation} \|F(S_x)\| \leq \|S_x\| \left(1+ \sum_{l=1}^{\infty} C_2^2\lambda_2^{2l} \right) = \|S_x\|\left(1+ C_2^2 \frac{\lambda_2^2}{1-\lambda_2^2}\right) = L'_2 \|S_x\|. \end{equation} Since $\beta$ and $\beta^{-1}$ are uniformly continuous, the right-hand side depends uniformly continuously on $x$, and hence $H_x \in U$.
nodes.statement_short: The series operator F on uniformly continuous families has norm L'_2.

nodes.name: Contraction
nodes.statement: Define the nonlinear operator $G:U \to U$ by $G(H_x) = S_x$, where $$ S_x = Z_x H^s_{\beta(x)}B^{su}_xH^s_x - Z_x B^{us}_x. $$ Similarly to Section \ref{sec:robust-Ak}, for small enough $\delta > 0$, $\varepsilon_2 > 0$ and $\|H_x\|, \|H'_x\| \leq \varepsilon_2$ we have $ \|GH_x-GH'_x\| \leq \frac{1}{2L_2'}\|H_x-H'_x\|. $ Since $F$ is linear, inequality \eqref{eq:FL'cont} implies that \begin{equation}\notag \|F \circ GH - F \circ GH'\| \leq L_2'\frac{1}{2L_2'}\|H-H'\| = \frac{1}{2}\|H-H'\|, \end{equation} According to \eqref{eq:Asux}, \eqref{eq:AB-ep1} and \textbf{(B2)} we have inequalities $\|G(H_x = 0)\| = \|Z_xB^{us}_x\| \leq CR\varepsilon_1$ and $ \|F \circ G (H_x = 0)\|\leq L_2'CR\varepsilon_1 $. Hence, there exists $H_x \in U$ with $\|H_x\| \leq 2L_2'CR\varepsilon_1$ such that $F\circ G (H_x) = H_x$, which implies \eqref{eq:H-via-Z}. Consequently, \eqref{eq:H-via-B} holds.
nodes.statement_short: F o G is a contraction on a small ball; its fixed point solves the equation.

nodes.name: Exponential estimates for stable spaces
nodes.statement: Proceeding as in \eqref{eq:B-proof}, by choosing $\varepsilon_1$ sufficiently small and, if necessary, decreasing $\delta$, we obtain generalized hyperbolicity estimates with exponent $\lambda_1$ for spaces $\tilde{E}_x^s$.
nodes.statement_short: Block argument gives rate lambda_1 on the new stable spaces.

nodes.name: Asymmetry of the unstable case
nodes.statement: Now we carry out the corresponding construction for $\tilde{E}^u_x$. Here, the stable and unstable cases are genuinely asymmetric, more so than in Lemma~\ref{lem:CL-robust-Ak}: there the operators are perturbed while the index shift $k \to k+1$ is common to $\mathcal{A}$ and its perturbation, whereas here the cocycle $A$ is fixed and the base map is perturbed, $\alpha \to \beta$. Time-reversal $A \to A^{-1}$ therefore does not turn the perturbed system into a base-only perturbation of the reversed original (its fiber map is sampled at $\beta^{-1}(x)$, not $\alpha^{-1}(x)$), so $H^s_x$ and $H^u_x$ act between genuinely different spaces and cannot be related by symmetry; this is what forces the auxiliary splitting at $\alpha(\beta^{-1}(x))$ introduced below.
nodes.statement_short: The unstable case is not symmetric; an auxiliary splitting is needed.

nodes.name: Condition for H^u
nodes.statement: In order to define $H^u_{x}: E_{\alpha(x)}^u \to A(x)E_x^s$ we need to establish an analog of \eqref{eq:Hsx-cond1}, i.e. to show that for any $\tilde{v}^u \in \tilde{E}^u_{\beta(x)}$ there exists $\tilde{w}^u \in \tilde{E}^u_{x}$ such that $ A(x)\tilde{w}^u = \tilde{v}^u $, equivalently, for any $v^u \in E^u_{\alpha(x)}$ there exists $w^u \in E^u_{\alpha(\beta^{-1}(x))}$ such that \begin{equation} w^u + H_{\beta^{-1}(x)}^uw^u = A^{-1}(x)(v^u + H_x^uv^u). \end{equation} Note that $$ H_{\beta^{-1}(x)}^uw^u \in A(\beta^{-1}(x))E^s_{\beta^{-1}(x)} \subset E^s_{\alpha(\beta^{-1}(x))}, \quad H_{x}^uv^u \in A(x)E^s_{x} \subset E^s_{\alpha(x)}. $$
nodes.statement_short: State the invariance condition for the unstable graphs.

nodes.name: Auxiliary splitting
nodes.statement: For small enough $\delta$ we have the splitting $\mathbb{B} = E^s_{\alpha(\beta^{-1}(x))} \oplus E^u_{\alpha(\beta^{-1}(x))}$. Denote by $\tilde{P}_x$, $\tilde{Q}_x$ the projections corresponding to this splitting. Similarly to the construction of $\tilde{E}^s_x$ define \begin{align*} {C}_x^{ss}: E_{\alpha(x)}^s \to \mathbb{B}, & \quad C_x^{ss} = \tilde{P}_{x}A^{-1}(x); &\qquad {C}_x^{su}: E_{\alpha(x)}^u \to \mathbb{B}, & \quad C_x^{su} = \tilde{P}_{x}A^{-1}(x);\\ {C}_x^{us}: E_{\alpha(x)}^s \to \mathbb{B}, & \quad C_x^{us} = \tilde{Q}_{x}A^{-1}(x); & \qquad {C}_x^{uu}: E_{\alpha(x)}^u \to \mathbb{B}, & \quad C_x^{uu} = \tilde{Q}_{x}A^{-1}(x). \end{align*} Note that since we considered the decomposition of $A^{-1}$, the operator $C_x^{ss}$ is ``expanding'' and the operator $C_x^{uu}$ is ``contracting''.
nodes.statement_short: Use the splitting at alpha(beta^{-1}(x)) and block operators of A^{-1}.

nodes.name: Equation for H^u
nodes.statement: Equation \eqref{eq:cond-Eu} is equivalent to $$ w^u = {C}^{uu}_x v^u + C^{us}_x H_{x}^uv^u, \quad H_{\beta^{-1}(x)}^uw^u = {C}^{su}_x v^u + {C}^{ss}_x H_{x}^uv^u. $$ Hence, the condition on $H^u$ is \begin{equation} H_{\beta^{-1}(x)}^u \circ \left( {C}^{uu}_x + C^{us}_x H_{x}^u \right) = {C}^{su}_x + {C}^{ss}_x H_{x}^u. \end{equation} Similarly to \eqref{eq:Zx-cond} define the operator $\tilde{Z}_x:E^s_{\alpha(\beta^{-1}(x))} \to A(x)E^s_x$ such that $\tilde{Z}_x \circ C^{ss}_x = Id_{A(x)E^s_x}$. Condition \eqref{eq:H-Eu-cond-1} is equivalent to \begin{equation} H_{x}^u = \tilde{Z}_x H_{\beta^{-1}(x)}^u {C}^{uu}_x + \tilde{Z}_x H_{\beta^{-1}(x)}^u C^{us}_x H_{x}^u -\tilde{Z}_x C^{su}_x. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to a fixed-point equation for H^u with right inverse tilde Z.

nodes.name: Solve for H^u
nodes.statement: Exactly as for \textbf{(B1)} and \eqref{eq:Zx-exp}, but using (C-GH3) for $A^{-1}$ in place of the estimates for $A$, for small enough $\varepsilon_1$ and some $C_2 > 0$ the contracting block $C^{uu}$ and the right inverse $\tilde{Z}_x$ satisfy \begin{equation}\notag \|C^{uu}_{\beta^{-(n-1)}(x)} \cdots C^{uu}_{\beta^{-1}(x)}C^{uu}_x\| \leq C_2\lambda_2^n, \quad \|\tilde{Z}_x \tilde{Z}_{\beta^{-1}(x)} \cdots \tilde{Z}_{\beta^{-(n-1)}(x)}\| \leq C_2\lambda_2^n, \quad n \geq 0,\ x \in \mathbb{B}. \end{equation} Hence \eqref{eq:H-Eu-cond-2} is the analog of \eqref{eq:H-via-Z} with $\beta, B^{ss}_x, B^{su}_x, B^{us}_x, Z_x$ replaced by $\beta^{-1}, C^{uu}_x, C^{us}_x, C^{su}_x, \tilde{Z}_x$, and the fixed-point argument for $H^s_x$ applies verbatim: for any $\varepsilon > 0$ and small enough $\delta$ there is an operator $H^u_x$ satisfying \eqref{eq:H-Eu-cond-2} with $\|H^u_x\| < \varepsilon$.
nodes.statement_short: Same contraction argument gives H^u with norm < epsilon.

nodes.name: Estimates and continuity of H^u
nodes.statement: The spaces $\tilde{E}^u_x$ satisfy the exponential estimates with exponent $\lambda_1$ as for $\tilde{E}^s_x$, via \eqref{eq:B-proof}. As in the construction of $H^s_x$ we prove that $H^u_x$ depends uniformly continuously on~$x$.
nodes.statement_short: Exponential estimates and uniform continuity for the unstable spaces.

nodes.name: Equality of sums
nodes.statement: Let us prove equality \eqref{eq:tildeE-EF}. According to construction $\tilde{E}^s_x \subset E^s_x \oplus F_x$ and \begin{align*} A^{-1}(x)\tilde{E}^u_{\beta(x)} & \subset A^{-1}(x)E^u_{\alpha(x)} \oplus A^{-1}(x)A(x)E^s_x = E^s_x \oplus F_x. \end{align*} Hence, \begin{equation} \tilde{E}^s_x \oplus A^{-1}(x)\tilde{E}^u_{\beta(x)} \subset E^s_x \oplus F_x. \end{equation} For any $x \in \mathbb{B}$ and $v^s_x \in E^s_x$ define the vectors $$ v^u_x := H^s_xv^s_x \in F_x = A^{-1}(x)E^u_{\alpha(x)}, \quad v^u_{\alpha(x)} := A(x)v^u_x \in E^u_{\alpha(x)}, \quad v^s_{\alpha(x)} := H^u_x v^u_{\alpha(x)} \in A(x)E_x^s. $$ Then $v^s_x + v^u_x \in \tilde{E}^s_x$ and $v^u_{\alpha(x)} + v^s_{\alpha(x)} \in \tilde{E}^u_{\beta(x)}$.
